starterQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', which characters are supernatural?
starterQuiz.hint: Look at the characters and work out where they live. Do they live in the magical forest, or in Athens?
starterQuiz.feedback: There are three main supernatural characters, along with a number of fairies. Oberon and Puck are the most important in terms of the plot as they create and restore the chaos in the forest.

starterQuiz.stem: What type of play is 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' includes the supernatural, but that is not how we define it.
starterQuiz.feedback: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' is designed to make its audiences laugh. It ends happily, and in a number of marriages, making it a comedy.

starterQuiz.stem: When we talk about Shakespeare's plays, we give them genres. What does genre mean?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that science fiction and tragedy are both genres.
starterQuiz.feedback: Knowing the genre of a particular text can help us understand what to expect from it, and also to enjoy if the writer does unexpected things within the genre.

options.text: the amount of humour in a text
the style or type of text

starterQuiz.stem: Shakespeare wrote just under 40 plays. What genre of plays did he write?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' includes an epilogue, but that is not a genre of play.
starterQuiz.feedback: In the first collection of Shakespeare's plays in 1623, his work was divided into tragedies, comedies and histories.

starterQuiz.stem: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' is a comedy. What are some of the key features of a Shakespearean comedy?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that intricate means complicated. Consider this plot of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'. Is it intricate?
starterQuiz.feedback: Shakespearean comedies are designed to make us laugh, and they usually do this through a plot that involves misunderstandings and physical comedy. 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' includes all the key features of a Shakespearean comedy.

options.text: They end in chaos and disorder.

starterQuiz.stem: A pupil said: "Shakespeare created the name and character of Puck/Robin Goodfellow". How would you correct them?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that Shakespeare knew his first audiences would engage and connect with Puck. How?
starterQuiz.feedback: The first audiences of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' had common beliefs about the supernatural, perhaps stronger beliefs than a more modern audience. The character of Robin Goodfellow was known for being mischievous but also helping with housework.

options.text: Robin Goodfellow was a well known figure in Elizabethan folklore.
Shakespeare stole these names from another playwright.
The word "puck" was a common name for an evil fairy in Elizabethan England.
The name Puck was famous, but he came up with Goodfellow to show Puck is kind.

exitQuiz.stem: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' is a {{}} whereas 'Macbeth' is a tragedy.
exitQuiz.hint: Consider this word defines one of the genres of Shakespeare's plays.
exitQuiz.feedback: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' contains all the key features of a comedy, with an intricate plot, misunderstandings, physical comedy and a plot that ends in a number of marriages.

exitQuiz.stem: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' includes supernatural characters. How do we know Shakespeare was interested in the supernatural more generally?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that when Shakespeare's plays were first published as a collection in 1623, they were divided into tragedies, comedies and histories.
exitQuiz.feedback: Shakespeare includes supernatural characters, events and settings in many of his plays. Sometimes the supernatural is presented as clearly evil, and sometimes its presentation is open to interpretation.

options.text: He stands out as the only Elizabethan interested in the supernatural.
His work is divided into tragedies, comedies and magical plays.
He created folklore about the supernatural.
He includes the supernatural in lots of his plays.

exitQuiz.stem: Some argue that Puck, a central character in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', is presented in an ambiguous way. What does this mean?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider the first two syllables of this word come from the Latin "ambi" meaning both ways.
exitQuiz.feedback: In many ways, Puck is a figure of fun and mischief. However, some of his actions and feelings could be interpreted as more cruel and Elizabethan ideas about fairies and the supernatural often connected them to the devil.

options.text: His character is loyal to Oberon.
His character is open to interpretation.
His character is famous in Elizabethan folklore.

exitQuiz.stem: It can be useful to compare different characters from different Shakespeare plays. In what ways are the witches in 'Macbeth', then, different to Puck in  'A Midsummer Night's Dream'?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that the witches spend time on stage creating a magical potion around a cauldron.
exitQuiz.feedback: Comparing the witches to Puck can help us understand how important Puck is to creating the comedy in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', not only because he makes the play funny, but because he also helps restore order so the play can end happily.

options.text: The witches never appear on stage; Puck is often on stage.
The witches lead to the tragic ending; Puck leads to the comic ending.
The witches obey no-one; Puck obeys Oberon.
The witches are presented as evil; Puck is more mischievous.
The witches have magical powers; Puck has to use a magical potion.

exitQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', in what ways is Puck presented as an ambiguous character?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider how the fairy introduces him in 2.1. She says he gives people "good luck" but also that he can frighten young women.
exitQuiz.feedback: The words in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' never change. However, what can change is how we, or an actor, interpret those lines, drawing attention to different things in the script. Puck's lines are particularly open to interpretation.

options.text: His actions can only be interpreted as harmless fun.
His actions can only be interpreted as evil.
He could be interpreted as mischievous or more malevolent.
He is only ever presented as loyal to Oberon.
His actions and words could be interpreted in a range of ways.

exitQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', in what ways is Puck central to making the play a comedy?
exitQuiz.hint: Shakespearean comedies share key features. What are those key features?
exitQuiz.feedback: Although Puck only speaks to the character of Oberon, he is key in terms of creating the intricate plot full of confusion and chaos. Equally, he is key in restoring order and making sure the play ends happily.

options.text: He has an epilogue at the end of the play.
He gets married at the end of the play.
He helps restore order at the of the play.
He creates a moment of physical comedy by transforming Bottom.

lessons.title: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream': powerful topic sentences about Puck

keyLearningPoints: Topic sentences state a paragraph’s main idea.
Evaluative topic sentences offer a judgement about a character.
You could compare one character to another, or the complexity of a character, to create an evaluative topic sentence.
Conjunctions can help create an evaluative topic sentence.
You must support your evaluative topic sentence with appropriate evidence from the text.

keywords.definition: the first sentence of a paragraph stating its main idea
to make a judgement about something
disrespectful
a word which connects two clauses in a sentence; for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so and although are all examples
insulting

starterQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', what do we know about the character of Egeus?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that Hermia chooses to run away from Athens.
starterQuiz.feedback: The play begins with Egeus telling Duke Theseus that he comes with "complaint" against his daughter Hermia. He is angry she wants to marry Lysander, rather than the man he has chosen for her. He threatens her with death if she doesn't obey him.

options.text: He threatens Lysander with severe punishments.
He threatens Hermia with severe punishments.
He banishes his daughter from Athens.

starterQuiz.stem: Puck and Egeus are both characters in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'. What are some of the differences between them?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider Puck's status in relation to Oberon. Where is he on the hierarchy?
starterQuiz.feedback: Comparing two characters can be a helpful way of understanding each deeper. Looking at the pain that Puck wants to inflict, compared to the punishment Egeus wants to inflict on his daughter perhaps puts Puck's pranks in perspective!

options.text: Puck is supernatural; Egeus is not.
Puck has a high status; Egeus does not.
Puck disobeys orders; Egeus follows them.
Puck likes to play harmless pranks; Egeus threatens severe punishments.
Puck is a servant; Egeus is a powerful patriarch.

starterQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', both Oberon and Puck use the magical potion. What are the differences between how they use it?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that Puck makes a mistake when he uses the magical potion on Lysander in Act 2, Scene 2.
starterQuiz.feedback: When Puck uses the magical potion on Lysander, he thinks he is Demetrius and is trying to make sure he falls in love with Helena. But when Oberon uses it on Titania, he says she hopes that she falls in love with something "vile".

options.text: Puck wants to create chaos; Oberon uses it for good.
Puck accidently causes chaos; Oberon deliberately harms Titania.
Puck uses it to transform Bottom; Oberon uses it to trick Titania.
Puck doesn't know what the potion can do; Oberon does.

starterQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', how do we know that Puck enjoys watching the Athenian nobles in chaos?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that Puck leads the Athenians through the forest to restore order.
starterQuiz.feedback: Puck calls the Athenian chaos a "fond pageant", meaning a funny show, and a "sport" meaning an enjoyable hobby. His reaction contrasts to Oberon's who is keen to restore order immediately.

options.text: He refuses to use the antidote as Oberon orders.
He leads the Athenians through the forest to increase their unhappiness.
He causes more chaos by putting the magical potion on Helena.
He says he finds watching unhappiness a fun hobby.
He asks Oberon if they can watch the chaos as entertainment.

starterQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', how do we know that Puck respects the hierarchy?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that Puck transforms Bottom in Act 3, Scene 1. What has he already done by this point?
starterQuiz.feedback: Despite being a mischief maker, Puck is presented as a very loyal servant both through his answers to Oberon's commands, and his actions which see him prioritise Oberon's wishes over his own.

options.text: He refuses to use magical potion Titania.
He obeys Oberon's orders swiftly and efficiently.
He obeys Oberon's orders even when he doesn't want to.
He shows respect to Egeus by using the magical potion incorrectly.
He only has fun with Bottom after he has fulfilled Oberon's orders.

starterQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', why might we describe Puck as a contemptuous character?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider this word means insulting or disrespectful.
starterQuiz.feedback: Puck respects Oberon, but he makes fun of almost every other character finding pleasure in their pain and humiliation.

options.text: He doesn't always listen to Oberon.
He disobeys Oberon when he finds something more fun to do.
He makes fun of the Rude Mechanicals.

exitQuiz.stem: When writing about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', you should start each paragraph with a clear {{}} which states the paragraph's main idea.
exitQuiz.hint: Consider this is a two word phrase and the first word is a synonym for subject.
exitQuiz.feedback: A topic sentence gives a paragraph purpose and drive. It directs your thinking and reminds you what you should be focusing on throughout your paragraph.

exitQuiz.stem: When writing about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', you could start paragraphs with a topic sentence. You must support this topic sentence in the paragraph. What does it mean to support a topic sentence?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that once you have stated your idea, you should develop rather than repeat it.
exitQuiz.feedback: A supported topic sentence will require you to select evidence from the text. This can be one of the most enjoyable parts of planning as you get to return to the text itself and choose significant moments from it to analyse!

options.text: To show why you could agree or disagree with the idea.
To show how you support the text you are reading.
To select quotations from the text you are writing about that prove your idea.
To list all the quotations you know from the text on this topic.

exitQuiz.stem: In this topic sentence about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', which word is the conjunction? "Shakespeare presents Puck as a mischief maker but his pranks are often harmless unlike Oberon's."
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that the word "presents" is the verb in this sentence.
exitQuiz.feedback: A conjunction can help complicate an idea that you have by developing it. In this way, you can make your sentences evaluative.

exitQuiz.stem: In this topic sentence about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', which word is the conjunction? "Although Shakespeare presents Puck as an irreverent character, to Oberon he only ever shows respect."
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that Shakespeare is a proper noun, not a conjunction.
exitQuiz.feedback: A conjunction can help complicate an idea that you have. Here, the word "Although" pushes you to write about two sides of Puck's character.

exitQuiz.stem: Which quotation would best support this topic sentence about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream': "Shakespeare presents Puck as a character who restores order despite his love of chaos."?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider which quotations best shows that Puck is key to restoring order.
exitQuiz.feedback: This quotation ends Act 3, Scene 2 and sees an end to the chaos in the forest. Puck's words come at the end of a rhyming song-like sequence of dialogue that is reassuring after the chaos of the Athenian's fighting.

options.text: "You are that shrewd and knavish sprite Called Robin Goodfellow." Act 2, Scene 1
"For now I must to Oberon." Act 2, Scene 2
"I am that merry wanderer of the night." Act 2, Scene 1
"I jest to Oberon and make him smile[.]" Act 2, Scene 1

exitQuiz.stem: Which quotation would best support this topic sentence about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream': "Shakespeare presents Puck as a character who is a devoted servant to Oberon despite his love of chaos."?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider which quotation shows Puck's responsiveness to Oberon's orders.
exitQuiz.feedback: This quotation comes from the first dialogue between Oberon and Puck. Unlike his long explanation of all the tricks he likes to play on people to the fairy, here Puck is almost silent and merely responds to Oberon's orders quickly and efficiently.

options.text: "You are that shrewd and knavish sprite Called Robin Goodfellow." Act 2, Scene 1
"Lord, what fools these mortals be!" Act 3, Scene 2
"I am that merry wanderer of the night." Act 2, Scene 1
"Shall we their fond pageant see?" Act 3, Scene 2
"I'll put a girdle round about the earth In forty minutes." Act 2, Scene 1

starterQuiz.stem: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' is a {{}}, which means it is a play designed to make you laugh, often involving misunderstandings and ending in marriage.
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that when Shakespeare's plays were first published in a collection known as the First Folio, they were divided into three genres: tragedies, histories and what other genre?
starterQuiz.feedback: Knowing the genre of the Shakespearean play you are reading or watching can help you predict what might happen, or some of the main features you might expect to find.

starterQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', the character of Puck is also know as...
starterQuiz.hint: Consider Puck is also known with a first and last name. The last name suggests he is a nice or kind man.
starterQuiz.feedback: Robin Goodfellow was a well known figure in Elizabethan folklore. He was known for his mischief, but also for helping with housework in exchange for a small fee.

starterQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', which characters does Puck speak to directly?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that when Puck interacts with Lysander, he is either asleep, or believes Puck's voice is that of Demetrius.
starterQuiz.feedback: Despite interacting with many of the characters, Puck only truly speaks to Oberon, the fairy and, in his epilogue, the audience. Perhaps this speaks to Oberon's control over his servant.

starterQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', what does Puck do for Oberon?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that transforming Bottom is Puck's own plan. He does it after trying to fulfil Oberon's orders about the magical potion and the Athenian nobles.
starterQuiz.feedback: Oberon's dialogue with Puck is often punctuated with orders which his servant fulfils as best he can. Exploring Puck's relationship with Oberon is a great way of thinking about Puck's characterisation.

options.text: steals the little boy Oberon wants from Titania
restores order to the unhappy Athenian nobles
puts the magical potion on Titania

starterQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', it could be argued that Egeus tries to control Hermia in some of the same ways that Oberon tries to control {{}}.
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that Oberon and Egeus are both presented as powerful patriarchs. Who do they exert their power over?
starterQuiz.feedback: Act 1 begins with conflict between father and daughter. Act 2 begins with conflict between two partners. Although there are differences, both Oberon and Egeus are presented as powerful patriarchs who feel their ultimate power has been undermined.

starterQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', why might we describe Puck as an irreverent character?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider this word is a synonym for disrespectful.
starterQuiz.feedback: Puck's irreverence, particularly towards the Rude Mechanicals, is balanced with his key role in restoring order at the end of Act 3, and his respectful attitude towards Oberon.

options.text: He enjoys chaos in the forest.
He restores order in the forest.

exitQuiz.stem: When writing about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' it is useful to understand the following terms. Match each to their definition.
exitQuiz.hint: Start with thesis. This is found in your introduction and you return to it throughout your paragraphs.
exitQuiz.feedback: Knowing these terms can help you understand what is required of you when you are asked a question about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'. An essay is a developed piece of extended writing which contains an idea you have about a text.

match.left: a piece of writing that explains and develops a big idea you have
an idea you develop and maintain throughout an essay
the first sentence of a paragraph which states its main idea

exitQuiz.stem: An analytical {{}} about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' will see you write a long answer to a question that explains and develops a big idea you have about a text.
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that this word comes from the French 'essayer' which means 'to try' or 'to attempt'.
exitQuiz.feedback: Develop your essay writing skills is a life long journey. They are incredibly rewarding things to plan, write and edit precisely because they are very challenging. You should feel very proud of every essay you write about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'.

exitQuiz.stem: When writing about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', you will create a thesis statement. What is true of thesis statements?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that in an essay, you will include one thesis statement but many topic sentences.
exitQuiz.feedback: Creating a thesis is one of the first steps when planning to write an essay. It is the foundation of your essay - the main idea you have about a particular character or theme in a text.

options.text: It is the first sentence of each paragraph stating its main idea.
It is found in your introduction.
It states the main idea you will prove throughout your essay.
It is a synonym for an essay.
It is found in your conclusion - a thesis is what you work towards.

exitQuiz.stem: When writing about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', you will create a thesis statement. How can you maintain ideas from your thesis throughout your essay?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that to maintain your thesis means to keep it going, to continue it.
exitQuiz.feedback: By creating a thesis, and then using your topic sentences to develop and maintain your thesis, you will create a powerful argument. This argument will be more powerful than if your essay is made up of lots of different but unconnected ideas.

options.text: By copying your thesis into every paragraph.
By using your topic sentences to develop your thesis.
By making sure your thesis is powerful.
By coming up with completely new ideas in every paragraph.
By arguing both sides of your thesis.

exitQuiz.stem: When writing about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', you will create a topic sentences. What is true of topic sentences?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that your topic sentences and thesis should be closely connected.
exitQuiz.feedback: Powerful topic sentences give a paragraph focus. Your topic sentences should be closely connected to your thesis so that your essay develops and maintains the big idea you set out in your thesis.

options.text: They are found in your introduction.
They introduce new ideas separate to your thesis.
They develop and maintain your thesis.
They come at the start of your paragraph and state the paragraph's main idea.

exitQuiz.stem: When writing about 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', you will create a thesis statement and topic sentences. What are some of the differences between them?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that a thesis statement is found in your introduction to an essay.
exitQuiz.feedback: Thesis statements and topic sentences help build an essay. They are important structural features. You establish your thesis in the introduction, and keep returning to it by developing it in topic sentences that start each paragraph.

options.text: A thesis statement starts your essay; topic sentences start a paragraph.
A thesis statement presents two sides to an argument; a topic sentence doesn't.
A thesis statement ends you essay; a topic sentence starts an essay.
A thesis statement explains if you liked the text; a topic sentence is analysis.
A thesis statement is your main idea; topic sentences develop your thesis.

starterQuiz.stem: Shakespeare has two settings in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'. What are they?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that Shakespeare's first audiences were English Elizabethans but he presents a different world to them on stage in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'.
starterQuiz.feedback: Acts 1 and 5 take place in the ordered city of Athens. Acts 2, 3 and 4 take place in the magical forest. It is here that much chaos, confusion and comedy occurs.

starterQuiz.stem: Shakespeare sets 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' in Athens and in a magical forest. What are some of the differences between the two places?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that Oberon and Titania are King and Queen of the forest. What does that suggest about whether it has a hierarchy or not?
starterQuiz.feedback: In many ways, Athens and the forest are different. Certainly, the chaos and confusion that occurs in the forest couldn't happen in the ordered world of Athens. It could also be interesting, though, to consider in what ways the settings are the same.

options.text: Athens is supernatural; the forest is not.
Athens has a hierarchy; the forest does not.
Athens is very structured and ordered; there is chaos in the forest.
Athens is ruled by humans; the forest is ruled by fairies.
There is no conflict in Athens; there is a lot of conflict in the forest.

starterQuiz.stem: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', what are some of the supernatural things that occur?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider which events are supernatural, and which are things which could be experienced by anyone.
starterQuiz.feedback: Shakespeare explores the power of the supernatural in his play (it can alter who you are, and who you love) but he also presents supernatural characters who are just like us - we, like the fairies, make mistakes and have fights.

options.text: the use of the magical potion
the conflict between Oberon and Titania
Lysander falling in love with Helena

starterQuiz.stem: Shakespeare wrote  'A Midsummer Night's Dream' for an Elizabethan audience. What were some of their views on the supernatural?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider a famous figure from Elizabethan folklore was Robin Goodfellow. What might his last name suggest about his character?
starterQuiz.feedback: Elizabethans had a strong interest in the supernatural and many of Shakespeare's plays explore the supernatural. Sometimes Shakespeare presents the supernatural as clearly evil but, in this play, its presentation is more ambiguous.

options.text: That the supernatural could be evil and connected to the devil.
That the supernatural only existed in plays and songs.
That fairies could be sometimes be kind and helpful.

starterQuiz.stem: Why might we describe the presentation of the supernatural in 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' as ambiguous?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that the word ambiguous means open to interpretation.
starterQuiz.feedback: Whilst the words in the script of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' never change, different people will interpret them in different ways. As such, some might consider the supernatural as malevolent, whilst others might see it as more mischievous.

options.text: Puck is clearly meant to be evil.

units.title: Taking a stand
units.description: In this unit, pupils learn about the different ways that writers have expressed their points of view across history. They look at some key techniques that writers use, such as motif and triad, before reading a speech, article, poem and song. They finally write and deliver their own presentation.

lessons.title: Expressing convictions
lessons.outcome: I can explain how writers express their convictions with passion.
keyLearningPoints: Throughout history, writers have used their skills to take a stand to address social issues.
Writers also use their skills to express their views with conviction and passion.
Sometimes a writer taking a stand can have real world benefits by stimulating awareness of an issue.
Different text types have different strengths when it comes to expressing convictions.
Writers make specific language choices to express their views strongly and effectively.

lessons.title: Aristotle's triad

keyLearningPoints: Aristotle was an influential ancient Greek philosopher who lived between 384 BCE to 322 BCE.
Aristotle wrote about politics, rhetoric and logic.
Aristotle’s triad consists of logos, ethos and pathos.
Logos is the appeal to reason; ethos is the appeal to authority and credibility and pathos is the appeal to emotion.
Aristotle’s triad is very important when planning persuasive writing.

the conflict is finally resolved

exitQuiz.stem: What was Charles Kingsley's profession?

exitQuiz.stem: What of the following best explains the popularity of stories about transformation?

options.text: They provide an escape from reality and allow readers to imagine other lives.

They depict dramatic conflicts and suspenseful plots that engage readers.

lessons.title: ‘Where Have All the Flowers Gone?’: a song of conviction
lessons.outcome: I can explain how structure and imagery can be used to take a stand.
keyLearningPoints: A poem can be turned into song and used to take a stand.
‘Where Have All The Flowers Gone’ is a famous anti-war song.
The song uses a cyclical structure to show the inevitability of war.
The imagery of flowers in the poem reflects the beauty and innocence that is destroyed by war.
Repetition of “where” and “learn” reinforces the sense of loss and history’s inability to teach us about violence.

keywords.definition: making you feel sad
feeling or expressing a deep sadness
to make something stronger
a short part of a song or poem that is repeated
something that shows a policy or system is bad or wrong

contentGuidance.label: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the best description of what lyrics are?

starterQuiz.feedback: Lyrics are often seen as a type of poetry.

options.text: a type of poetry with a set rhythm and meter
the melody or musical composition of a song
the emotional atmosphere created by a piece of music

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is a synonym for "mood"?

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of the context of a text?

the social and historical background of a text
the language and structure of a text

starterQuiz.stem: In literature, we often say that 'a thing' can represent an idea.  Which of the following is the best definition of represent?

options.text: to pretend to be the thing

starterQuiz.stem: In literature, imagery means...
starterQuiz.hint: Which option relates to things you can see?
starterQuiz.feedback: Imagery is one of the most vivid ways that writers engage our interest.

options.text: the sequence of events in a story
the underlying message of a story to teach the reader something
the use of language designed to create pictures in the reader's mind
the overall structure of a text

exitQuiz.stem: Who wrote the poem and song 'Where All The Flowers Gone?'?
exitQuiz.hint: His first name is Pete.
exitQuiz.feedback: Peter Seeger was a folk singer and activist and transformed a poem into an anti war song.

exitQuiz.stem: Match the words on the left with the synonyms on the right.

exitQuiz.feedback: Indictment is a useful word to know when discussing writers who take a stand. Often they are writing to show that something is wrong or bad.

match.left: moving, touching
sad, sorrowful
to strengthen
accusation

exitQuiz.stem: In the following title, 'Where Have All the Flowers Gone?' which word evokes a sense of loss or that something is missing and cannot be found?
exitQuiz.hint: Which word is a question and therefore suggests something can't be found if the speaker is asking?

exitQuiz.stem: What word beginning with r refers to a line or phrase that is repeated throughout a poem?
exitQuiz.hint: The first three letters are "ref".

exitQuiz.stem: In the following title, 'Where Have All The Flowers Gone?' which word represents beauty and youth?
exitQuiz.hint: Which of the words refers to something growing?

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following explains the use of structure in 'Where Have All the Flowers Gone?'?

options.text: The cyclical structure reinforces the sense of war being ever ending.
The cyclical structure reinforces the innocence of the young people.

lessons.title: Creating content for a formal presentation
lessons.outcome: I can understand how to use a range of skills to take a stand and create a formal presentation.
keyLearningPoints: Creating content for a presentation can mean using facts, experts and an appropriate tone to take a stand.
A metaphor involves the transfer of qualities from one thing to another.
An extended metaphor will help direct your choice of vocabulary throughout the presentation.
An effective way to structure your presentation is to begin and end in the same place.
Presenting visual ideas at the start of a presentation can be very impactful.

keywords.definition: move from one place to another
add to something to make it larger or longer
a group of words linked by a common theme
the quality of forming a unified whole
a strong effect or influence

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the follwoing is the best definition of an opinon?

starterQuiz.feedback: Expressing your opinion means to speak or write about what you personally think and believe in.

options.text: a personal belief or point of view
a point of view shared by everyone
a scientific theory tested through experiments

starterQuiz.stem: Which is the best definition of the word 'unified'?

starterQuiz.feedback: Writing needs to be unified meaning it works together as a whole.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of 'linguistic skills'?

options.text: the ability to write 'hello' in multiple languages
the ability to say 'hello' in multiple languages
competency in understanding and using language effectively
knowledge of the grammatical rules of English

starterQuiz.stem: To add to something to make it larger or longer is to {{}} it.

starterQuiz.stem: The structure of a text refers to ...
starterQuiz.hint: Which option refers to arrangement?
starterQuiz.feedback: Learning how to structure your writing for effect will help you write with impact.

options.text: the font and formatting used in the text.
the language used by the writer.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is a synonym for 'pollution'?
starterQuiz.hint: The word begins with a C.
starterQuiz.feedback: Contamination is a useful word for writing about both illness and environmental damage.

exitQuiz.stem: Match the words on the left with their synonyms on the right.
exitQuiz.hint: Start with transfer. It has the same prefix as transport.
exitQuiz.feedback: Coherent writing and an extended metaphor are two skills that you can use to create effective writing.

match.left: move
lengthen
unity
effect

exitQuiz.stem: When creating a metaphor, we are imaginatively transferring {{}} from one thing to another.
exitQuiz.hint: The word begins with a Q.
exitQuiz.feedback: Creating a metaphor is an act of imaginative transference in which the qualities of the thing being compared onto the thing being described.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of an extended metaphor?
exitQuiz.hint: Something that is extended is stretched out.
exitQuiz.feedback: An extended metaphor is an effective and very visual way of unifying your writing.

options.text: a brief comparison between two things that are very different
a metaphor that continues over several sentences, paragraphs or lines
a metaphor that is used once very strikingly in a piece of writing
a metaphor which is simple and easy to understand

exitQuiz.stem: Which three of the following words could belong in a semantic field?
exitQuiz.hint: Which options belongs in the area of football? They create a semantic field of football when put together.
exitQuiz.feedback: A semantic field groups words with similar meanings. A semantic field can be very effective when unifying a text.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following uses a visual metaphor?
exitQuiz.hint: Which option refers to something we can see?
exitQuiz.feedback: All the options are metaphors, but only option 2 draws on the sense of sight.

options.text: The problem is a disease that we can all catch.
The problem is a bruise on society's skin.
The problem is a terrifying cry in the dark.

exitQuiz.stem: Why is it important to reflect on the skills we have learned?
exitQuiz.hint: Which two options are both kind and supportive?
exitQuiz.feedback: It is good to take time to reflect on your progress.  That way, you can see what you already know and create plan for improvement.

options.text: to identify and acknowledge what we can do
to self criticise so we stop making mistakes

lessons.title: Planning content for a presentation
lessons.outcome: I can generate ideas and plan a presentation.
keyLearningPoints: A presentation can be used for a variety of purposes.
It can be useful to sum up your idea in a one sentence statement of the presentation's key message.
You should be clear about the who, what, when and how of your presentation.
A plan is essential if you are going to write effective content for your presentation.

keywords.definition: able to judge fairly because you are not influenced by your own opinion
influenced by personal feelings
important events that are happening in the world
to speak on behalf of a person or group who needs help with representation
causing disagreement or discussion

starterQuiz.stem: What is the best definition of an article?
starterQuiz.hint: Look at the options that relate to things which are real.
starterQuiz.feedback: An article is non fiction and it might use key events, but it does more than just record them.  It will usually explore them in detail. .

options.text: a short story in a magazine
a piece of writing that records key events
a non-fictional prose text about a specific topic
a fictional narrative written in the first person

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is a the best synonym for 'opinion'?
starterQuiz.hint: Which one sounds most personal?
starterQuiz.feedback: Other synonyms for opinion are point of view and viewpoint.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the best description of a social issue?
starterQuiz.hint: Which option refers to the largest group of people?
starterQuiz.feedback: A social issue is a problem that is bigger than the individual and exists on a national and even global level.

starterQuiz.stem: If something is a challenge, it is ...
starterQuiz.hint: Which option sounds like the most unpleasant?
starterQuiz.feedback: Another synonym for "challenge" would be difficulty.

starterQuiz.stem: When you generate ideas, what are you doing?
starterQuiz.hint: Which one sounds as if it would bring about new ideas?
starterQuiz.feedback: There are many ways of generating ideas. One of them is using questions to get you thinking.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the best reason for making a plan before you start writing?
starterQuiz.hint: Which option is about putting ideas in order?
starterQuiz.feedback: The best writing always starts with a plan.

options.text: A plan helps you remember what you intend to write.
A plan makes you better at writing.
A plan helps you organise your ideas.
A plan helps you use SPaG more effectively.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following refers to someone who speaks on behalf of someone or a group?
exitQuiz.hint: The word begins with an A.
exitQuiz.feedback: Advocacy is the term for the work done by an advocate.

exitQuiz.stem: What word beginning with 'C' refers to an issue that is likely to cause disagreements?
exitQuiz.hint: The first three letters are 'con'.
exitQuiz.feedback: The noun is controversy. A controversy is an issue that causes disagreement.

exitQuiz.stem: Starting with the first, organise the stages of an article so they are in chronological order.

order.text: strong start
effect on you
effect on people around youe
effect on society
back to the beginning

exitQuiz.hint: Look at the phrases that include a verb.
exitQuiz.feedback: Words like "immediate", "pressing" and "critical" are synonyms for "urgent".

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the best reason for using specific criteria when we plan our writing?
exitQuiz.hint: Which option is aimed at ensuring we do our best work?
exitQuiz.feedback: A criteria can be a useful measure of how well we have done and what we still need to do.

options.text: to ensue we follow guidelines and reach a good standard
to add complexity to the writing process
to discourage people from being controversial

exitQuiz.stem: It is important to note down the tone you will use in your writing. What do we mean by tone?
exitQuiz.hint: Which option most relates to atmosphere?
exitQuiz.feedback: Tone refers to  how we speak or write.  For example, we might express our ideas in an angry tone or an outraged tone.

options.text: the author's opinions, beliefs or ideas
the way the text is organised
the mood or moods of a text
the way an article starts and ends

lessons.title: Preparing to deliver a presentation
lessons.outcome: I can use effective preparation strategies to help me deliver a presentation confidently.
keyLearningPoints: Presentations are much more engaging when the speaker does not simply read off a page or memorise word for word.
Effective cue cards will give just the right amount of information to help to deliver and structure a presentation.
If you take questions, try and respond with new content rather than repeating parts of the presentation.
Asking open questions can invite developed responses.
If you are unsure how to answer a question, using tentative phrases can help.

keywords.definition: a small card used during a speech or presentation to help the speaker remember key points or prompts
to make guesses or predictions about something
with reference to delivering a presentation, this means speaking in a relaxed way without scripts
something that is uncertain or not fully decided

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of a challenge?
starterQuiz.hint: Which one will involve most effort but can be resolved?
starterQuiz.feedback: Challenges ask a lot of us, but they can also be an opportunity to prove ourselves.

options.text: an obstacle that cannot be overcome
a difficult task that tests our abilities
a simple and 'easy to solve' problem
a problem that will resolve itself

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is a synonym for focus?
starterQuiz.hint: Which one refers to thinking deeply?
starterQuiz.feedback: When we are focused on something, we pay attention to small details.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the word for the top of a mountain?
starterQuiz.hint: This word begins with an 'S'.

starterQuiz.stem: What word beginning with 'P' describe the different sections of an article or formal piece of writing?

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following uses a verb in the imperative form?

starterQuiz.feedback: Using imperatives can be an effective way of engaging your reading and inspiring them to action.

Why won't he roll up his sleeves and get started?

exitQuiz.stem: What word beginning with 'e' describes a metaphor that runs throughout a text?

Maybe we could consider an alternative.

options.text: ignore our mistakes until very end.
write swiftly and decisively ensuring we finish in time.
consider what works well and how to improve.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following is a call to action?

For more information on this issue, visit our website
Join us in this fight against this issue.

lessons.title: Delivering a formal presentation

keyLearningPoints: Body language and eye contact support the successful delivery of a presentation.
Gesture and posture can be used to engage the audience and to add emphasis to important points.
Spoken language often needs to be slower than feels natural.
You need to consider your spatial behaviour- too much movement can be distracting but too little can be wooden.
It's okay to feel nervous, find the strategies that work for you.

keywords.definition: non-verbal cues or gestures such as facial expressions and posture

movements of the body (especially hands or arms) to express ideas or emotions
refers to the way someone holds themselves when they're seated or standing

starterQuiz.stem: What is the purpose of creating cue cards for a speech?

starterQuiz.stem: What type of questions invite developed responses, rather than just a 'yes' or 'no'?

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is a synonym for 'magnificent'?

starterQuiz.stem: Which word beginning with 'c' describes a small card used during a speech or presentation to help the speaker remember key points or prompts?
starterQuiz.hint: The homophone (a word that sounds the same, but is spelled differently) of this word is 'queue'.
starterQuiz.feedback: Creating and using cue cards is an effective way to prompt you, when delivering your presentation. It can help create a more naturalistic and engaging delivery.

starterQuiz.stem: Which is the best definition of the term 'sophisticated vocabulary'?

options.text: a collection of words on the same theme
a vocabulary that includes technical terms and jargon
a vocabulary full of colloquial expressions

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following would you use to show confidence when delivering a speech?

exitQuiz.feedback: Considering these elements will ensure a confident presentation delivery.

exitQuiz.stem: When delivering a speech your eye contact should be ...

exitQuiz.feedback: You should look at your audience generally, varying your eye contact to generate greater engagement.

exitQuiz.stem: Which word can be used to describe the non-verbal cues or gestures such as facial expressions and posture in spoken language?

exitQuiz.stem: With reference to delivering a presentation, which word means speaking in a relaxed way without scripts?

exitQuiz.feedback: Aiming to deliver the presentation in a naturalistic way can help to engage your audience.

exitQuiz.stem: Which word beginning with 'p' can be described as the way someone holds themselves when they're seated or standing?

exitQuiz.feedback: Gesture and posture can be used to engage the audience and to add emphasis to important points.

units.title: Single poet study: Maya Angelou
units.description: In this unit, pupils read and discover the work of Maya Angelou. They explore some of Angelou's most famous poems, such as 'Caged Bird' and 'Still I Rise', and practise writing and performing poems inspired by her work. As the unit develops, pupils find their own distinctive poetic voice.
threads: Modern literature strand 1: identity, belonging and community

lessons.title: An introduction to Maya Angelou's distinctive voice: ‘Life Doesn’t Frighten Me’
lessons.outcome: I can explore Maya Angelou's 'Life Doesn’t Frighten Me' with a focus on the speaker's distinctive voice.
keyLearningPoints: Maya Angelou (1928-2014) was an American poet and civil rights activist.
Angelou's poems have a distinctive voice.
Figurative language, repetition and an assertive tone are three ways Angelou creates a distinctive voice in her work.
Arguably, the speaker in 'Life Doesn’t Frighten Me' is presented as assertive.
You could argue that the speaker in 'Life Doesn’t Frighten Me' is only pretending to be assertive.

keywords.definition: a person who advocates for social and political equality for those who have been denied equal treatment
non-literal phrases or words which develop a writer's meaning
the tools a writer uses to create their work; repetition and figurative language are just two examples
something that is appealing and interesting because of its recognisable or special qualities
confident, self-assured

equipment: You need access to a copy of 'Life Doesn’t Frighten Me' by Maya Angelou published by Penguin Random House in 1993.

contentGuidance.label: Depiction or discussion of discriminatory behaviour
contentGuidance.description: Discriminatory behaviour or images, whether on the grounds of race, gender, disability, religion or belief or sexual orientation, or otherwise.

contentGuidance.label: Depiction or discussion of discriminatory behaviour
contentGuidance.description: Historic or outdated representations of people that may portray inequality or injustice.

starterQuiz.stem: What is a stanza? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that a stanza is a bit like a poetic paragraph.
starterQuiz.feedback: A poem is a type of text that expresses feelings and ideas. Often these feelings or ideas are divided into stanzas. When reading a poem, you can consider how many stanzas it has, and what each one focuses on.

options.text: a poet's use of rhyme in a poem
a verse of grouped lines in a poem

starterQuiz.stem: Maya Angelou was born in St Louis, Missouri. Which continent is this in? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that the Missouri is in the northern hemisphere.
starterQuiz.feedback: Missouri is a state in the midwestern region of the United States. It is landlocked which means it is bordered by other states rather than being on the coast.

starterQuiz.stem: Match each technique to its definition. ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that 'My mind is an ocean' is an example of a metaphor.
starterQuiz.feedback: These techniques are examples of tools writers can use. Simile and metaphor are probably the hardest to create. When you see a great example, spend time considering why it's so powerful – it's the first step to creating your own impressive examples!

match.left: the intentional recurrence of a word or phrase
using the verb form to give an order e.g. stand up
comparing two things using 'like' or 'as'
comparing two things using the verb 'to be'

starterQuiz.stem: Which of these are examples of commands? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that a 'command' is a synonym for an 'order'.
starterQuiz.feedback: A writer's use of commands in their work can be really interesting. It might tell us about a particular character, or create a particular tone. Have you read any poems that use commands? Who are they commanding? You, the reader? Or someone else?

options.text: Don't only eat chocolate for lunch.
I stood boldly in front of them.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of these is an example of a simile? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that a simile is a method of comparison – it is not just about using the words 'like' or 'as'.
starterQuiz.feedback: Similes are tricky to write – there are lots that are over used (e.g. I'm as cool as a cucumber). You want to be original. Give yourself time when crafting a simile. Experiment with different ideas and don't expect your first to be your best!

options.text: The bird didn't like being trapped in its cage.
As far I'm concerned, she's a phenomenal woman.
Her eyes burned with the fire of a thousand suns.
I will never give up; like the sun, I will always rise to fight another day.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of these are examples of metaphors? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that a metaphor, like a simile, is a method of comparison. However, it does not use the words 'like' or 'as'.
starterQuiz.feedback: Metaphors are tricky to write – there are lots that are over used (e.g. The teacher was a dragon). You want to be original. Give yourself time when crafting a metaphor. Experiment with different ideas and don't expect your first to be your best!

options.text: Her eyes were ablaze: pure liquid fire.
My body is an ocean – powerful and strong.
I am always going to fight for equality.
She sang like a song bird.

exitQuiz.stem: Match each method to its definition ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that describing yourself as an ocean, or that your eyes are like fire are examples of figurative language.
exitQuiz.feedback: These are just three of the methods that Maya Angelou often relies upon in her work to create a distinctive voice. Why not look at one of her poems and see if you can see how she uses these methods?

match.left: the intentional recurrence of a word or phrase
words that reveal the speaker to be confident and self-assured
non-literal phrases or words which develop a writer's meaning

exitQuiz.stem: What award did Angelou receive from President Barack Obama in 2011? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider this award is not only given for being an excellent writer.

lessons.title: Writing a poem inspired by Maya Angelou's 'Life Doesn't Frighten Me'

keyLearningPoints: Maya Angelou uses stanzas and a refrain to structure her poem, 'Life Doesn't Frighten Me'.
'Life Doesn't Frighten Me' uses monosyllables at points for effect.
You can use a poet's work to inspire your own creativity.
You can plan each stanza of a poem by considering its focus and the details, including the methods, you want to include.
Reading your poem aloud can help you identify areas you would like to improve.

starterQuiz.stem: What type of text is Maya Angelou's 'Life Doesn’t Frighten Me'? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider what it looks like on the page, and how it sounds when you read it out.
starterQuiz.feedback: A poem is a type of text that expresses feelings and ideas. There is a close attention to how each word, line and stanza sounds – that's why it often a really good idea to read a poem aloud!

starterQuiz.stem: Which of these is a synonym for the word shake? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that the word shake tells you about how someone moves.
starterQuiz.feedback: In English, there are so many words that have synonyms, but each synonym has a slightly different meaning. Having a wide vocabulary means you can select the exact word you want to express your particular idea.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of these things does the speaker in Maya Angelou's 'Life Doesn’t Frighten Me' not mention?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that the speaker does mention school, but only focuses on the other people in her class.
starterQuiz.feedback: There are a range of different things that the speaker says do not frighten her but heights isn't one of them.

starterQuiz.stem: Starting with the first, put what is said in Maya Angelou's 'Life Doesn’t Frighten Me' in chronological order. ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that the poem ends with a repetition of the title.
starterQuiz.feedback: Looking at a poem and thinking about the journey – how it starts, what happens in the middle, how it ends – can be a great step to understanding it more deeply.

order.text: The speaker says she is not scared of things like shadows and noises.

starterQuiz.hint: Consider that what scares the speaker is not an object or person.
starterQuiz.feedback: There are many things that the speaker says they aren't scared of, but there is a tiny admission of vulnerability near the end of the poem – the speaker says "if" she is ever scared, it's in her dreams. Why do you think Angelou includes this detail?

starterQuiz.stem: How many times does Maya Angelou repeat the title 'Life Doesn’t Frighten Me' in the poem itself? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that the title is used as a refrain. This means it is repeated more than once.
starterQuiz.feedback: Maya Angelou uses the title as a refrain, which means it is a bit like a chorus in a song that is repeated multiple times. Consider why you think Angelou chose to do this.

exitQuiz.stem: In 'Life Doesn’t Frighten Me', which of these is the refrain? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that a refrain is a repeated line or set of lines in a poem.
exitQuiz.feedback: Maya Angelou chooses to repeat her title multiple times in her poem. You could consider what effect this has, and then try out this method in your own work.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of these words are monosyllabic? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that a monosyllabic word has one beat. A polysyllabic word has many syllables. For example, Angelou has three syllables: Ang-el-ou.
exitQuiz.feedback: Monosyllabic words can often have a powerful effect. They can give a poem a powerful beat, slow down the pace of a poem, or provide a contrast to words with many syllables. Why not try writing some monosyllabic words for effect in your next poem!

exitQuiz.feedback: Literal language is, of course, very useful and is necessary for lots of different text types. But poetry is often written in the opposite of literal language – in figurative language – so that writers can develop complex ideas and images.

lessons.title: Performing Maya Angelou's ‘Still I Rise’
lessons.outcome: I can perform one stanza of Maya Angelou's 'Still I Rise' with a focus on conveying the speaker's power.
keyLearningPoints: There is a contrast between the way the speaker and those who have oppressed her are presented in 'Still I Rise'.
When performing a poem, you should consider how you want to engage with your audience.
You should make informed decisions about the pace, volume and tone of your voice.
You should aim to know your material off by heart so you can look at the audience most of the time.

starterQuiz.stem: One of Maya Angelou's poems is called 'Still I {{ }}' ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
starterQuiz.hint: Consider this word means to get up.
starterQuiz.feedback: The word "rise" is deceptively simple. Although the idea of getting up is completely normal, in this poem, the word "rise" is a metaphor for overcoming the oppression that the speaker has faced. It is a powerful, positive and awe-inspiring verb.

starterQuiz.stem: What word does Maya Angelou's 'Still I Rise' start with? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that the verb is the final word in the first stanza, and the final word of the whole poem.
starterQuiz.feedback: This word "you" is repeated a number of times, particularly in the first stanza. It seems accusatory, and sets up an opposition between the speaker and those who have sought to oppress her.

starterQuiz.hint: Consider that many of the similes compare the speaker to natural things.
starterQuiz.feedback: Angelou is a master of comparison, often connecting her speakers to powerful objects or ideas that help us understand their strength. Why not read one of Angelou's poems and see if you can identify a powerful simile?

starterQuiz.stem: A {{ }} question is a question that is used for dramatic effect, rather than one expecting an answer ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
starterQuiz.hint: Consider this word comes from the Greek 'rhetor' meaning 'an orator' (public speaker).
starterQuiz.feedback: Many poets use rhetorical questions in their work. They can increase the drama, but also make a direct connection to the reader or the audience if they are performing their work. Why not try to use a rhetorical question in your next poem!

exitQuiz.hint: Consider that you want to be able to look at your audience as much as possible. What would enable you to do this?
exitQuiz.feedback: Good performance is all about the preparation. You should make informed decisions about how you want to say your piece. In addition, knowing your material by heart means you can look at your audience, an important way of connecting with them.

exitQuiz.stem: What does it mean to project your voice? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that this word comes from the Latin 'pro-' meaning 'forth', and 'jacere' meaning 'to throw'.
exitQuiz.feedback: This word comes from the Latin 'pro-' meaning 'forth', and 'jacere' meaning 'to throw'. This etymology helps us understand what it means – you are 'throwing' your voice so that it reaches the very edges of your audience.

exitQuiz.stem: What is the final word of Maya Angelou's poem 'Still I Rise'? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that the first word is an example of direct address (speaking directly to the reader).
exitQuiz.feedback: The poem goes on a journey, starting with the pronoun "you" but ending with the speaker doing something (rising). In this way, the speaker balances the accusations she makes to her oppressors, with her triumph over them.

exitQuiz.stem: Does Angelou use rhetorical questions in 'Still I Rise'? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that the questions often start or end with the word "you".
exitQuiz.feedback: Angelou relies on rhetorical questions for dramatic effect in her poem. The questions are accusations, and reveal the full horror of what her oppressors have done to her, and how they wish her to act.

options.text: Yes: she asks her oppressors questions.
Yes: she starts the poem with a rhetorical question.
No: the questions are meant to be answered.

exitQuiz.stem: How does the speaker describe herself in Maya Angelou's 'Still I Rise'? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider the speaker uses powerful, positive terms for herself.
exitQuiz.feedback: Angelou balances the way the speaker feels about herself, with the way she perceives her oppressors. We get a picture of a powerful, resilient speaker and resentful, cruel oppressors.

exitQuiz.stem: The speaker in Maya Angelou's 'Still I Rise' says her oppressors tell lies about her. How does she describe these lies? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that these words both use plosives (repetition of letters p, t, k, b, d, g) for effect.
exitQuiz.feedback: Angelou carefully chose these words to convey the cruel and disgusting nature of the lies her oppressors have told about her. The word "twisted" is a metaphor, describing the lies as distorted, unnatural things.

lessons.title: Exploring Maya Angelou's 'Caged Bird'
lessons.outcome: I can explore Maya Angelou's 'Caged Bird'.
keyLearningPoints: An extended metaphor is a detailed comparison which develops one idea over a number of lines, paragraphs or stanzas.
In 'Caged Bird', the idea of a bird in a cage is an extended metaphor for the unjust experiences of the Black community.
In 'Caged Bird', Angelou is perhaps referencing the racial segregation enforced by the 19th-20th century Jim Crow laws.
When comparing two poems, it can be useful to first think about what connects them.
After finding a point of connection between poems, you could consider the differences within this point of connection.

lessons.title: Performing Maya Angelou's ‘Caged Bird’

keyLearningPoints: When performing a poem, you should make informed decisions about the pace, volume, and tone of your voice.
Your pace, volume and tone could be very different at different moments of the poem.
Experimenting with different ways of saying a poem can be a good way to decide on how you ultimately want to perform it.
You will also want to consider body language and eye contact when performing a poem.
When you don't know a poem by heart, you should consider how to maintain a good level of eye contact with your audience.

lessons.title: Exploring Maya Angelou's 'Equality'
lessons.outcome: I can explore Maya Angelou's 'Equality'.
keyLearningPoints: 'Equality' sees a speaker demand equality so that she can be "free".
Arguably, the poem presents racial and gender inequality that Angelou experienced as a Black American woman.
'Equality' starts with the word "you" and we could argue that the speaker has an accusatory tone at points in the poem.
Arguably, the speaker's response to the inequality she sees makes it a poem about resilience in the face of inequality.
Linking quotations together when you explore a poem can make your idea more powerful.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of these words are synonyms for 'literal'? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that "I walked to the shops quickly." is literal but "I flew to the shops." is not.
starterQuiz.feedback: Literal language is factual. Its opposite is figurative language which expresses meaning in a non-literal way. For example, in 'Still I Rise', the speaker compares herself to an "ocean". She is not literally an ocean, but it expresses her power.

starterQuiz.feedback: Writers, particularly poets, often use figurative language in their work. This means they use language to express deep, complex meanings. Metaphors, similes, personification and exaggeration are all examples of figurative language.

exitQuiz.feedback: This metaphor expresses how the speaker doesn’t feel like they are treated as an equal member of her society. A "shadow" is not given the same rights as a human.

exitQuiz.stem: How old was Angelou when 'On Aging' was first published? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that the collection was published at what many think of as a significant age.
exitQuiz.feedback: Angelou's 'On Aging' was published in 1978 when she was 50. In the UK, 50 is often thought of as a significant age which is perhaps why Angelou chose to reflect on the idea of getting older.

exitQuiz.hint: Consider that to depose someone means to remove them from power.
exitQuiz.feedback: In many of Angelou's poems, her speakers are not self-deprecating. Instead, they express their power and confidence. However, in 'On Aging', the speaker does make some jokes about how she moves and acts now she is older.

exitQuiz.stem: In 'On Aging', how does the speaker describe herself at the start of the poem? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that the speaker creates a humorous tone with this description.
exitQuiz.feedback: Angelou describes herself as a "sack" at the beginning of the poem which creates a funny image of an undignified person. However, the speaker than says she doesn't want sympathy or help just because she looks like this – she is happy sitting alone.

exitQuiz.stem: In 'On Aging', how does the speaker describe herself at the end of the poem? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that the speaker repeatedly says she doesn't want any sympathy.
exitQuiz.feedback: The speaker describes herself as "lucky" at the end of the poem because she can breathe. This is another example of the humour in the poem: the speaker says that growing older is hard but she feels lucky that she is at least still alive!

exitQuiz.stem: 'On Aging' was published in 1978 in Maya Angelou's collection called 'And Still I Rise'. What other poems were published in this collection? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that 'Equality' was first published in 1990.
exitQuiz.feedback: Angelou wrote many collections of poetry and many autobiographies. Knowing which poems were published together, and under what title, can sometimes give insight into what was particularly important to Angelou at that point in her career.

You must hear my cry: we need equality.
I am a remarkable woman, and it's time you saw that.
The bird in the cage sang loudly.

starterQuiz.stem: How many stanzas does Maya Angelou's 'On Aging' have? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')

starterQuiz.feedback: Before writing a poem, poets consider how many stanzas they need to convey their ideas. Look at your favourite poem. How many stanzas does it have? What is the focus of each stanza?

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the sentences below are examples of figurative language? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that figurative language is the use of non-literal phrases and words which develop a writer's meaning.
starterQuiz.feedback: Angelou uses lots of figurative language in her poems to express complex emotions and ideas. For example, in 'Still I Rise', we get a sense of the speaker through comparison to things like the "ocean" or "suns".

options.text: I walk with confidence and grace.
I stomp elephant-like into the room.
I thundered out of the room, a storm cloud of anger.
I left the room hastily, but elegantly.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of these Angelou poems uses first person? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider first person means using pronouns like "I" and "me".
starterQuiz.feedback: Just like in other texts, in poems you can use first, second or third person. In the main, Angelou uses first person. This often makes us feel connected to the speaker in the poem.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of these Angelou poem titles uses figurative language? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that figurative language is the use of non-literal phrases and words which develop a writer's meaning.
starterQuiz.feedback: 'On Aging', 'Phenomenal Woman' and 'Equality' are all titles which state, literally, what the poem will be about. 'Caged Bird' is a metaphor, as is the title 'Still I Rise'.  The speaker is not literally "rising". The bird in the cage is a metaphor.

exitQuiz.stem: Which sentence is an example of sibilance? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that "The song soared sweetly through the silent crowd." is another example of sibilance.
exitQuiz.feedback: Sibilance is the repetition of the 's' sound in a set of words. It is sometimes used to create a menacing atmosphere.

options.text: The small child stuck his tongue out and stared.
It was a silly thing to do.
I looked longingly at the lolly.

exitQuiz.stem: Which sentence is an example of alliteration? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that "Don't drive me down with your deliberate lies." is another example of alliteration.
exitQuiz.feedback: Alliteration is the repetition of the same letter at the beginning of a group or words. Alliteration can be particularly important in poetry because the way poems sound aloud is very important to many poems.

options.text: Life may be scary, but I'm not frightened.
I am powerfully and persistently phenomenal.
I won't be forgotten or mistreated.
Save your silly songs for someone stupid.

exitQuiz.stem: When editing your work, reading your piece of writing {{ }} can help you hear what sounds good, and what needs further work ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider this way of reading is the opposite of reading in your head.
exitQuiz.feedback: Reading your work aloud – any work, not just a poem – is a great way of hearing what is good about it, and what needs further work. It helps you hear rhythm, but also grammatical mistakes.

exitQuiz.stem: Which sentence uses the word sullen, or its forms, correctly? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that sullen means bad-tempered, sulky.
exitQuiz.feedback: Having a wide vocabulary helps you write imaginatively and precisely. If appropriate, use the word sullen, or its forms, in your next piece of writing.

options.text: Angelou's speakers are often uplifting, rather than sullen.
If I am feeling sullenly, I often read a poem to lift my spirits.
I was pleased to help; that's why I looked so sullen.
Angelou uses a sullen number of stanzas in 'Still I Rise'.

exitQuiz.stem: Which sentence uses the word idle, or its forms, correctly? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that idle means not doing anything, lazy.
exitQuiz.feedback: Idelist is not a word. The adjective is idle. Having a wide vocabulary helps you write imaginatively and precisely. If appropriate, use the word idle, or its forms, in your next piece of writing.

options.text: I ran to school idly because I didn't want to be late.
I was accused of being idly, but I was just thinking.
I hate being idle – I'm always up and about doing something.
I was idelist this morning so I didn't make my bed.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of these sentences uses the word ignoble correctly? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that ignoble means not honourable.
exitQuiz.feedback: Having a wide vocabulary helps you write imaginatively and precisely. If appropriate, use the word ignoble, or its forms, in your next piece of writing.

options.text: He called me ignoble, which I think is unfair. I am always lying and cheating.
I was ignoble this morning so I had a huge breakfast.
He seemed ignoble to me and I didn't trust him.
Robbing the bank was ignoble, but what choice did I have?

lessons.title: Refining poems: harmony and dissonance
lessons.outcome: I can refine a poem by paying close attention to its harmony and dissonance.
keyLearningPoints: Poets pay close attention to how their poems sound, as well as what the words express.
You might like a poem for its harmonious sound before you understand its meanings.
Angelou created harmonious sounds in her poems, often relying on rhythm, rhyme, repetition and refrain.
When writing your own poems, reading your work aloud lets you to hear what sounds harmonious, and edit dissonant sounds.

the beat, flow, or pattern of a piece of music or writing

in music, a combination of sounds that don't sound nice.

starterQuiz.stem: Maya Angelou wrote a poem called 'Still I {{ }}' ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
starterQuiz.hint: Consider this word is a synonym for getting up.
starterQuiz.feedback: The poem's title is a metaphor. The speaker says that, despite all the oppression she has faced – past and present – she will overcome it and remain a powerful presence.

starterQuiz.stem: What is the refrain in the Maya Angelou's poem 'Still I Rise'? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that a refrain is a repeated line or set of lines in a poem.
starterQuiz.feedback: Angelou often relies on refrains in her poems. They repeat a central idea, the main message of the poem that Angelou doesn't want her audiences to forget. Refrains are often particularly powerful in performance.

starterQuiz.stem: How many syllables does the word rhyme have? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that a syllable is the number of beats in a word. The word 'poetry' has three syllables.
starterQuiz.feedback: When writing a poem, poets play close attention to the length of each line and the poem's rhythm. One way to do this is to consider how many syllables each word, and therefore each line, has.

starterQuiz.stem: How many syllables does the word harmony have? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that a syllable is the number of beats in a word. The word 'poem' has two syllables.
starterQuiz.feedback: When writing a poem, poets play close attention to the length of each line and the poem's rhythm. One way to do this is to consider how many syllables each word, and therefore each line, has.

starterQuiz.stem: What books did Maya Angelou have next to her when writing her poems? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that one book was a religious one.
starterQuiz.feedback: Maya Angelou had a strict writing routine, hiding away in a rented hotel room with minimal distractions. She had a dictionary and a Bible. Consider why you think she might have found these books so helpful.

exitQuiz.stem: How many syllables does the word dissonance have? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that a syllable is the number of beats in a word. The name Angelou has three syllables.
exitQuiz.feedback: When writing a poem, poets play close attention to the length of each line and the poem's rhythm. One way to do this is to consider how many syllables each word, and therefore each line, has.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of these words is a synonym for rhythm? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that tone is about the emotion in your voice – written or verbal.
exitQuiz.feedback: Consider a song you like. Part of what makes you like it is the way it sounds – its rhythm. This is the same with poetry. Poems are meant to sound nice, as well as express interesting emotions. Enjoying a poem's rhythm is a great way into a poem.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of these words is the best antonym for dissonance? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that a syllable is the number of beats in a word; for example, "rise" has one syllable, "history" has three syllables.
exitQuiz.feedback: The opposite of dissonance is harmony. In music, we look for harmonious sounds – sounds like are nice together. It is the same in poetry. We are looking for words and phrases which sound nice together.

exitQuiz.stem: Maya Angelou read her work out loud after writing in order to hear any "{{ }}". ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that this word is an antonym for harmony.
exitQuiz.feedback: For Angelou, reading her work aloud was an important part of the writing process. It helped her hear what needed work to sound better (less dissonant, more harmonious).

exitQuiz.stem: Which of these sentences uses the word harmony, or its forms, correctly? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that harmony is not a synonym for good.
exitQuiz.feedback: Harmony is a word we often associate with music. Instruments and voices create harmony. Meetings can be harmonious if everyone agrees with each other. 'Disharmonious' is not a word.

options.text: I was pleased with the song: it had a harmonious melody.
Everyone left because the song sounded disharmonious.
We had a harmonious meeting: everyone agreed with each other.
He asked if I wanted to go, and I said harmoniously.
My teacher said my essay was very harmony.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of these sentences uses the word dissonant, or its forms, correctly? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that undisonant is not a word.
exitQuiz.feedback: Having a wide vocabulary helps you write imaginatively and precisely. If appropriate, use the word dissonance, or its forms, in your next piece of writing.

options.text: He asked if I wanted an ice-cream and I said dissonantly not.
I couldn't barely hear the music because the volume was so dissonant.
I put my hands over my ears to block out the dissonant sounds.
The poem needed work: some lines were dissonant.
The song sounded great: undisonant and rhythmical.

lessons.title: Finding my own voice: performing a poem
lessons.outcome: I can consider different aspects of performance and apply them to a performance of my own.
keyLearningPoints: When performing a poem, you should make informed decisions about the pace, volume and tone of your voice.
Your pace, volume and tone could be very different at different moments of a poem.
Experimenting with different ways of saying a poem can be a good way to decide on how you ultimately want to perform it.
You will also want to consider body language and eye contact when performing a poem.
When you don't know a poem by heart, consider how you will maintain a good level of eye contact with your audience.

keywords.definition: not honourable, unworthy
the attitude of emotion of your voice - written or verbal
not doing something, lazy

starterQuiz.stem: What is true of Maya Angelou? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that Angelou performed for Bill Clinton. Who is Bill Clinton?
starterQuiz.feedback: Angelou knew that, often, a good way to enjoy a poem is to read it aloud. As such, she performed many of her poems to huge audiences who loved the rhythm, rhyme and sound of her poems.

options.text: She performed a poem for a President.
Only her poems with refrains are meant to be read aloud.
She read her work aloud as part of her editing process.
Her poems are meant to be set to music.
Performance was important to her work.

starterQuiz.stem: Which poem did Maya Angelou write and perform for Bill Clinton? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Consider the title of this poem suggests a new start.
starterQuiz.feedback: Angelou was asked to write and perform at President Bill Clinton's inauguration – a huge honour. She chose to write about America, and won a Grammy for her performance!

starterQuiz.stem: Match each element of performance to its explanation ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
starterQuiz.hint: Consider what the word pace means in other areas of life. For example, in running.
starterQuiz.feedback: Good performance is all in the preparation. Those who think about all of these different elements of performance will create a performance that engages their audience.
