starterQuiz.stem: When you come across a piece of punctuation like a comma or a full stop when reading a poem aloud, what is the punctuation telling you to do? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
starterQuiz.hint: Read these two sentences: "She walked off. I wasn't upset." What do you do when you see the full stop?
starterQuiz.feedback: All punctuation tells the reader to pause briefly. We pause for a full stop for a longer period of time than any other punctuation mark.

starterQuiz.stem: A {{ }} is a repeated line or set of lines in a poem ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
starterQuiz.hint: Consider that in Maya Angelou's 'Life Doesn't Frighten Me', the title is an example of this.
starterQuiz.feedback: Angelou uses refrains in many of her poems. Often, they convey her central message that she wants her readers or audiences to remember.

exitQuiz.stem: What is good advice for someone who is preparing to perform a poem? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider the performances you have seen – singers, actors, poets. What do they have in common?
exitQuiz.feedback: A good performance is all in the preparation. Those who think about all of these different elements of performance will create a performance that engages their audience.

options.text: Look down at the poem throughout.
Engage the audience with eye contact.

exitQuiz.stem: What does it mean to vary your pace when performing a poem? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider what the word pace means in other areas of life.
exitQuiz.feedback: Varying your pace, as opposed to speaking at the same pace, will interest your audience and emphasise certain parts of the poem. Before performing a poem, consider which parts would sound best at a slower pace, and which at a faster.

options.text: to sometimes speak fast, and sometimes slow

exitQuiz.stem: What does it mean to vary your tone when performing a poem? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou').
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that you would vary your tone to say these two different sentences: "Hurry, you're making me late!" and "How many scoops of ice cream would you like?"
exitQuiz.feedback: Varying your tone is one of the best ways to engage your audience. You can, just with your voice, convey a whole range of emotions which bring the poem alive. Why not reread an Angelou poem and vary your tone appropriately throughout?

options.text: to use gestures and body language
to sometimes speak fast, and sometimes slow
to alter the attitudes and emotions in your voice

exitQuiz.stem: What happened after Maya Angelou performed 'On the Pulse of the Morning' at President Clinton's inauguration? ('Single poet study: Maya Angelou')
exitQuiz.hint: Consider that President Clinton's inauguration was in 1993 when Angelou was already an established poet.
exitQuiz.feedback: Millions and millions of people watched Angelou perform 'On the Pulse of the Morning' in January 1993. The way in which she performed the poem was widely praised, and she won a Grammy for Best Spoken Word that year.

options.text: She won the Nobel Prize for literature.

I idle better than my sister.

exitQuiz.feedback: Having a wide vocabulary helps you write imaginatively and precisely. If appropriate, use the word 'ignoble', or its forms, in your next piece of writing.

units.title: Victorian childhood: non-fiction reading and writing
units.description: In this unit, pupils read a mixture of contemporary and nineteenth-century non-fiction texts that explore a common theme of childhood. They first read and compare the texts, before then writing and delivering a speech as part of a debate on Victorian working class children.

lessons.title: Exploring the experience of child workers in the Victorian era
lessons.outcome: I can read summarise different attitudes towards child labour in the Victorian era.
keyLearningPoints: Attitudes towards child labour were less strict in the Victorian era.
There are more laws today than in Victorian Britain to protect children from unsafe working conditions.
Young boys from lower social classes were expected to do dangerous jobs in the Victorian era.
Comparative conjunctions are useful for connecting sentences to previous ideas.
Comparisons are useful when comparing differences between authors’ attitudes or ideas.

keywords.definition: work, particularly physical work, can be referred to as labour.
if you force or oblige someone to do something, you compel them to do it.
a chimney sweep was someone who would clean the channel above a fireplace, which takes smoke out of buildings.
callous people have a cruel disregard for others.
a mercenary is primarily concerned with making money at the expense of ethics.

equipment: You will need access to a copy of ‘Child Workers, their rights and wrongs’ by Jon Robins which is available in the additional materials.

starterQuiz.stem: The Victorian era was named after which monarch?
starterQuiz.hint: Most eras are named after the the first name of the monarch who reigned at the time.
starterQuiz.feedback: The Victorian era was named after Queen Victoria.

starterQuiz.stem: A social class is a group in society with similar wealth and opportunities. Which of the following social classes would be more likely to be wealthy and hold power in society?
starterQuiz.hint: Which of the words 'working', 'ruling' or 'lower' implies you have more control?
starterQuiz.feedback: The ruling class (monarchs and governments) would be more likely to hold power and live more comfortable lives.

starterQuiz.stem: What does a chimney sweep do?
starterQuiz.hint: Chimney sweeping was a dangerous profession.
starterQuiz.feedback: Chimney sweeps often had to squeeze into small spaces to clean the inside of chimneys.

options.text: Chimney sweeps clean up any mess made when chimneys are built.
Chimney sweeps clean inside the chimneys, removing soot and debris from fires.
Chimney sweeps worked in stately homes, keeping the grand fireplaces tidy.

starterQuiz.stem: When did the Victorian era begin?
starterQuiz.hint: These dates represent the starts of the reigns of Queen Victoria, Queen Elizabeth I and Queen Elizabeth II. Do you know in what order they reigned?
starterQuiz.feedback: Queen Victoria's reign began in 1937 and lasted until 1901.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the definition of callous? Here it is used in a sentence: the callous man refused to help the girl.
starterQuiz.hint: Use this extra sentence to help you define it: the callous bully picked his next victim.
starterQuiz.feedback: Callous is a synonym for cruel, more specifically used to describe people who do not care about others.

starterQuiz.stem: What does the verb 'to compel' mean? Here it is used in a sentence: the teacher compelled the pupils to comply with the rules.
starterQuiz.hint: Use this extra sentence to help you define it: I was compelled to go, even though I didn't want to.
starterQuiz.feedback: If you feel compelled to do something, it means you feel obliged, as if you have no other option.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following skills should you use before reading a complex text?
exitQuiz.hint: Which of these four skills can you do without having read the text?
exitQuiz.feedback: You should always use clues available to you, such as the title, to make predictions about the text.

exitQuiz.stem: Which word, beginning with l, is a more formal way of saying 'child workers'?
exitQuiz.hint: A British political party, set up for the workers of Britain, is named after this word.
exitQuiz.feedback: The verb 'to labour' means to work very hard.

exitQuiz.stem: How would you describe Victorian attitudes to protecting child workers in comparison to attitudes today?
exitQuiz.hint: Would children be allowed to be chimney sweeps in Britain today?
exitQuiz.feedback: Victorians definitely had a less strict attitude towards child labour. In particular, boys from lower social classes were deemed suitable for dangerous work.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following is **not** a comparative conjunction which indicates a similarity between ideas.
exitQuiz.hint: Look out for root words in each phrase which mean similar or alike. These should help you find the odd one out.
exitQuiz.feedback: Nonetheless means 'in contrast to something that happened or was said.'

exitQuiz.stem: Which **two** comparative sentence stems are most useful for indicating a very clear difference in ideas?
exitQuiz.hint: Try inserting each sentence stem into the following sentence to see which works best: [Sentence stem] some Victorians were happy for working class children to undertake dangerous work, it is illegal for children to do dangerous jobs in Britain today.
exitQuiz.feedback: 'Despite' can be used to indicate some similarity, even when discussing differences.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following most accurately paraphrases the sentence: 'boys were inveigled out of the poorhouses'?

lessons.title: Education for poor Victorian children
lessons.outcome: I can explain how emotive language is used to discuss poverty in Victorian Britain.
keyLearningPoints: There was no compulsory schooling in Victorian Britain.
Education was a luxury only the rich could afford.
Ragged schools were designed to provide education to the poorest in society.
When analysing a writer's language choices, topic sentences should focus on effect rather than subject terminology.
Topic sentences which focus on effect give opportunity to make connections between quotations from across a text.

illiteracy means being unable, or struggling, to read and write.
destitute means extremely poor and unable to look after oneself.
a plea is a request made in an urgent or emotional manner.
ragged schools were schools which provided education to children who were too poor to receive it elsewhere.

units.title: A monster within: reading and writing Gothic fiction
units.description: In this unit, pupils explore the Gothic. They start by learning what the Gothic is, before reading extracts from 'Frankenstein' and 'Jane Eyre', practising descriptive writing and reading 'The Tell-Tale Heart'. They finally learn how to write opinion articles and then write their own.

lessons.title: Context for Gothic literature: science and religion in the 19th century
lessons.outcome: I can explore important contextual ideas that impact Gothic literature, focusing on the Enlightenment, the Industrial Revolution and Charles Darwin’s ‘On the Origin of Species’.
keyLearningPoints: The Enlightenment period represents a philosophical shift in thought, whereby reason and rationale were celebrated.
There was an emphasis on learning the ‘truth’ about things; people thought this would bring them knowledge and freedom.
The Industrial Revolution occurred in Britain in the 18th century, and then again in the 19th century.
Galvanisation is the process of using electricity to try to create life.
Scientific advancements were contested by religious people, who dismissed them as heresy.

starterQuiz.stem: When was 'Jane Eyre' published?

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following colours are considered to be Gothic colours?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider the symbolism of these colours. What do we associate them with?

starterQuiz.stem: Which weather might be expect to see in Gothic texts?

starterQuiz.stem: Who is Mr Rochester in 'Jane Eyre'?

starterQuiz.feedback: Mr Rochester is Jane's employer at Thornfield. She slowly falls in love with him and they end up getting married at the end of the novel.

starterQuiz.stem: Complete the sentence: The novel 'Jane Eyre' is written from a {{ }} person perspective.

exitQuiz.stem: How is Thornfield described in Chapter 12 of 'Jane Eyre'?

exitQuiz.feedback: Thornfield is described as a remote and dark setting in Chapter 12 of 'Jane Eyre'.

exitQuiz.stem: Complete the sentence: In Chapter 12 of 'Jane Eyre', Brontë {{ }} the "crimson" sun with the "pale moon" to create a Gothic setting.
exitQuiz.hint: The missing word means: To position two opposite things close to one another to draw attention to their difference.
exitQuiz.feedback: In Chapter 12 of 'Jane Eyre', Brontë contrasts the "crimson" sun with the "pale moon" to create a Gothic setting.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following would we not expect to see in a Gothic setting?
exitQuiz.hint: Remember that Gothic literature aims to unsettle its readers, so which of these might not unsettle a reader?
exitQuiz.feedback: We would not expect to see bright, colourful walls in a Gothic setting.

exitQuiz.stem: What is the effect of Brontë using the moon in her Gothic setting in Chapter 12?
exitQuiz.hint: How do people feel about the moon? How do some people respond to a full moon?
exitQuiz.feedback: Brontë includes the moon in her setting arguably to give the setting a supernatural quality and to play on people's superstition to characterise the setting as ominous to foreshadow the significant meeting between Jane and Rochester.

options.text: it makes the setting lighter because the moon's light shines
it gives the setting a supernatural quality
the moon is a figure of superstition, so it makes the setting ominous

exitQuiz.stem: What method does Brontë use in the following quotation from Chapter 12 of 'Jane Eyre'? "On the hill-top above me sat the rising moon; pale... she looked over Hay..."
exitQuiz.hint: Can a moon 'look' with its eyes?
exitQuiz.feedback: Brontë uses personification to characterise the moon as watchful, adding to the secretive and mysterious mood of the setting.

exitQuiz.stem: What is the effect of Brontë's word choice "hush" in the quotation from 'Jane Eyre': "it was yet a mile distant, but in the absolute hush I could hear plainly its thin murmurs of life"?

exitQuiz.feedback: The word "hush" not only illustrates Jane's isolation (as she can barely hear the nearby village) but also has connotations of secrecy, which allows Brontë' to create an atmosphere of mystery and intrigue.

options.text: the fact that the noises are muffled shows Jane's isolation
"hush" reflects Jane's quiet and subservient nature
"hush" is an informal word, which reflects Jane & Rochester's informal meeting
"hush" has connotations of secrecy, which makes the atmosphere mysterious
"hush" reflects Jane's nervousness when she meets Rochester for the first time

starterQuiz.stem: Who wrote 'Jane Eyre'?

starterQuiz.stem: The novel 'Jane Eyre' was set in the {{ }} era.

options.text: close - they share a very loving relationship
distant - they do not see much of one another
tense - Aunt Reed was cruel to Jane as a child

exitQuiz.feedback: The gardens at Lowood are extremely regimented and controlled. Brontë uses the gardens to show us the oppressive nature of the school.

to make the reader feel unsettled and uncomfortable
to mystify and intrigue the reader

exitQuiz.stem: What is the effect of Jane asking Mrs Fairfax about ghosts at Thornfield Hall in 'Jane Eyre'?

exitQuiz.hint: Gothic texts are supposed to give the reader an exciting, but disturbing experience.
exitQuiz.feedback: Refusing to reveal what you are describing until the very end can help you to build tension by keeping your reader guessing, the creating a thrilling and exciting experience for your reader.

options.text: to create a thrilling experience for the reader
to make your reader confused about the text
to build tension by withholding information
to foreshadow later events to come

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following sentences uses the word 'congealed' correctly?
exitQuiz.hint: If something congeals, it begins to change from a liquid state to a more solid state.
exitQuiz.feedback: The word 'congealed' is a great word to use if you want to create a horrifying description of blood.

options.text: She was so angry that congealed tears fell from her eyes.
The burger began to congeal as it started to ooze liquid.
The jelly-like substance had begun to congeal, forming horrible clumps.
The torrential rain congealed as it pummelled the pavement.
The dog snarled, congealed spit flying towards me as it did so.

lessons.title: Editing descriptive writing based on ‘A monster within’
lessons.outcome: I can edit, revise and rewrite my descriptive writing.
keyLearningPoints: Editing is the process of making technical corrections to a piece of writing.
Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar is essential to help your reader understand your writing.
Revising is where you look at or consider again a piece of writing in order to correct or improve it.
Using a variety of sentence starters is important because it can influence the pace, emphasis or cohesion of a sentence.
You can vary your sentence starters by using adjectives, verbs or adverbs.

keywords.definition: to make technical corrections to a piece of writing
to review a piece of work and identify where it can be improved
a version of a piece of writing
the process of rewriting sentences, adding, dropping or reframing ideas and choosing more precise words
to improve the quality or clarity of something

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following are verbs?
starterQuiz.hint: Verbs are 'doing' or 'having' words.
starterQuiz.feedback: "Am" and "be" are both verbs that students tend to forget.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following are adjectives?
starterQuiz.hint: Adjectives describe nouns.
starterQuiz.feedback: Combine adjectives together to create a more vivid picture for your reader.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following are adverbs?
starterQuiz.hint: Adverbs often end in 'ly', but not always.
starterQuiz.feedback: Even though it ends in 'ly', 'ugly'is not an adverb - it is an adjective because it describes a noun.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following verbs are in the present tense?
starterQuiz.hint: Use each of these verbs in a sentence to work out which tense they belong to.
starterQuiz.feedback: It is important to be able to recognise tense so that you can ensure your use of tense is consistent in your writing.

starterQuiz.stem: One of these verbs is in a different tense from the others. Which one is it?
starterQuiz.hint: All, but one of these verbs are in the past tense. Which verb is in the present tense?
starterQuiz.feedback: "Enter" is in the present tense. We might say "I watch him enter the shop."

starterQuiz.stem: Choose the most appropriate verb to complete the following sentence: __________ cautiously forward, I felt my heart rate quicken and my breathing become shallow.
starterQuiz.hint: Which of these best creates an ominous and foreboding atmosphere?
starterQuiz.feedback: The sentence "Creeping cautiously forward, I felt my heart rate quicken and my breathing become shallow" builds tension as we see the narrator's response to something horrifying or anxiety-inducing.

exitQuiz.stem: {{ }} is the process of reframing ideas and choosing more precise words.
exitQuiz.hint: You can only undertake this process when you have a first draft of your work.
exitQuiz.feedback: It is important to rewrite your work to ensure you have the best possible draft of your work to submit.

exitQuiz.stem: {{ }} is the process of making technical corrections to a piece of writing.
exitQuiz.hint: An example of this process might be making sure that all of your sentences begin with a capital letter.
exitQuiz.feedback: Editing includes addressing errors in capitalisation, punctuation, and grammar or lack of clarity in syntax.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following is an example of 'rewriting'?
exitQuiz.hint: Rewriting is the process of reframing ideas and choosing more precise words.
exitQuiz.feedback: Here, swapping the word 'crept' for the word 'advanced' is an example of rewriting because it is a decision the writer has made about their word choices.

options.text: adding an apostrophe into 'Emily' to make 'Emily's'
swapping the word 'crept' for the word 'advanced'

exitQuiz.stem: Complete the following sentence by adding in the correct verb: "I was so annoyed with myself. If I'd just applied myself, I could __________ been great!"
exitQuiz.hint: Only one is grammatically correct.
exitQuiz.feedback: 'Could of' is gramatically incorrect. Many students struggle with this. It is always 'could have'.

exitQuiz.stem: Identify the incorrect spelling, punctuation or grammar in the following sentence: "The gates rusty hinges were definitely close to the end of their miserable existence."
exitQuiz.hint: This is a punctuation issue.
exitQuiz.feedback: The word 'gates' is missing a possessive apostrophe because the hinges belong to the gate, so it should be 'the gate's rusty hinges'.

exitQuiz.stem: Identify the incorrect spelling, punctuation or grammar in the following sentence: "The forest's darkness chills me to my spine as I strained my eyes vainly in a desperate attempt to sea."
exitQuiz.hint: Check every word really carefully when you read the sentence. Consider the spelling, the punctuation and the grammar. Read the sentence aloud a few times.
exitQuiz.feedback: 'Chills' and 'strained' are in different tenses. 'Chills' is in the present tense and 'strained' is in the past tense. These need to match. Also 'see' is spelled incorrectly. 'Sea' and 'see' are homophones, so the wrong homophone has been used.

lessons.title: Reading 'The Tell-Tale Heart'
lessons.outcome: I can explain the overarching plot of the 'Tell Tale Heart'.
keyLearningPoints: ’The Tell-Tale Heart’ is the story about the murder of an old man.
The narrator did not murder for money but for fear of the man's blue eyes.
The narrator kills the man as he worries a neighbour may hear the loud beating of his heart.
The narrator dismembers the body and hides it under the floorboards.
The narrator continues to hear the beating heart of the dead man, which leads him to confess.

keywords.definition: suspicion and mistrust of other people or their actions that is not rational
taking a systematic and organised approach to something
pretence - hiding one’s true thoughts or feelings
being of sound and sensible mind
holding irrational or untrue beliefs - in this context, as a result of mental illness

equipment: You will need access to a copy of Edgar Allan Poe's 'The Tell-Tale Heart' for this lesson. It's available in the additional materials.

starterQuiz.stem: Gothic protagonists are usually egotistical and ....
starterQuiz.hint: Think about the protagonist Victor Frankenstein from 'Frankenstein.' What is he like?
starterQuiz.feedback: Gothic protagonists are usually isolated and/or egotistical. For example, in 'Jane Eyre', Jane is an isolated protagonist.

starterQuiz.stem: What can the colour yellow symbolise?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider the colour symbolism of yellow in 'Frankenstein' when it used to describe the Creature.
starterQuiz.feedback: The colour yellow can represent betrayal or illness, as seen in Gothic descriptions in both 'Frankenstein' and 'Jane Eyre'.

starterQuiz.stem: Which century was 1843 in?
starterQuiz.hint: Remember, to work out the century, add 1 to the two numbers at the beginning of the date.
starterQuiz.feedback: Edgar Allan Poe's 'The Tell-Tale Heart' was published in 1843, which was in the 19th century.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following statements is true about the 19th century?
starterQuiz.hint: Consider texts like 'Frankenstein' and 'Jane Eyre' (which were both published in the 19th century). What can we learn about the 19th century from these texts?
starterQuiz.feedback: Gothic literature was hugely popularised in the 19th century, though there are examples of Gothic texts from earlier, such as 'The Castle of Otranto' which was published in 1764.

options.text: The 19th century was also known as the Enlightenment period
The 19th century saw the first Industrial Revolution
Gothic literature was popularised in the 19th century
The 19th century was a time of great innovation and invention

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following words might mean 'to take a systematic and organised approach to something'?
starterQuiz.hint: An organised approach to something is also known as a method.
starterQuiz.feedback: Taking a methodical approach ensures that fewer mistakes are made.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following explains the effect of this quotation: "He had the eye of a vulture—a pale blue eye, with a film over it."
starterQuiz.hint: First, decide whether you think the eye is presented positively or negatively. This will narrow the answer options down for you.
starterQuiz.feedback: Vultures are considered repulsive creatures, who feed on the carcasses of dead animals. By using this simile, the writer presents the eye as hideous and repulsive.

options.text: The eye is presented as beautiful and enchanting
The eye is presented as repulsive and hideous
The eye is presented as vulgar and offensive
The eye is presented as extremely ordinary and usual

exitQuiz.stem: Who wrote 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
exitQuiz.hint: This writer had quite a difficult personal life.
exitQuiz.feedback: Edgar Allan Poe wrote 'The Tell-Tale Heart' in 1843.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following statements is true about short stories?
exitQuiz.hint: Focus on the word 'short'. What distinguishes a short story from a novel?
exitQuiz.feedback: Edgar Allan Poe wrote lots of short stories, many of which are considered classics in the Gothic genre.

options.text: they are more popular in the United Kingdom than America
you should be able to read one in between 20 and 60 minutes
each word has to work extra hard, so writers have to craft them very carefully
they are easier to write than novels

exitQuiz.stem: What nationality was Edgar Allan Poe?
exitQuiz.hint: Edgar Allan Poe was born in Boston. Where is Boston?
exitQuiz.feedback: Edgar Allan Poe was a successful and popular American author of Gothic stories and poems.

exitQuiz.stem: What drives the narrator in Poe's 'The Tell-Tale Heart' to commit murder?
exitQuiz.hint: The narrator is presented as delusional. His reason for murdering the old man shows his delusion.
exitQuiz.feedback: The narrator tells us that  "it was not the old man who vexed [him], but his Evil Eye".

options.text: his desire for the old man's money
a fear of the old man's pale, blue eye
his hatred of the old man, who is frequently rude to him
his dislike of himself and jealousy of the old man

exitQuiz.stem: Why does the narrator in 'The Tell-Tale Heart' confess to his crimes?
exitQuiz.hint: The narrator tells us: "[the police] heard!—they suspected!—they knew!—they were making a mockery of my horror!—"
exitQuiz.feedback: The narrator's confession is arguably further evidence of his insanity and delusion.

options.text: he gets pleasure from relaying his crimes to others
he wants to go to prison to protect others
he is convinced that the police already know he committed the crime
he feels extremely ashamed and remorseful for what he has done
he believes he hears the sound of the old man's heart -this makes him frenzied

exitQuiz.stem: Starting with the first,  put the events of 'The Tell-Tale Heart' in chronological order.
exitQuiz.hint: Start by identifying the reason as to why the narrator commits murder. Why does he want to kill the old man?
exitQuiz.feedback: The narrator's delusions escalate as the story progresses, thereby allowing Poe to build tension in the lead up to the narrator's confession.

order.text: The narrator tells us about his hatred of the old man's 'evil eye'.
The narrator sneaks into the old man's room seven nights in a row.
On the 8th night, the narrator accidentally wakes the old man up.
The narrator chuckles at the thought of the old man's fear.
The narrator thinks he hears the old man's heart beating, so he kills him.
The police visit, but they are unaware that the body is under the floorboards.
The narrator hears the old man's heart beating and hysterically confesses.

lessons.title: The creation of suspense in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'
lessons.outcome: I can identify the methods used by Poe to create suspense.
keyLearningPoints: The narrator in the story is extremely hubristic, unreliable and unpredictable because he is delusional.
Poe uses the hubristic and delusional narrator to create suspense.
Poe uses irony to create suspense - the narrator insists that he is not ‘mad’ but his actions suggest otherwise.
Poe shortens his sentences and uses more expressive punctuation to reflect the narrator’s escalating delusion.
Poe uses sentence structure and punctuation to build tension in the lead up to the narrator's dramatic confession.

keywords.definition: a state of feeling anxious or excited about what could happen
excessively proud or arrogant
not to be relied or depended on
extremely wicked
the expression of meaning by using language that suggests the opposite of the reality

starterQuiz.stem: What does the narrator in 'The Tell-Tale Heart' reveal about himself in the first line of the story?
starterQuiz.hint: This is the first thing the narrator tells us about himself. We suspect it may be a lie.
starterQuiz.feedback: The fact that the narrator begins the story by reassuring us that he is not mad, gives us the impression that he might be.

options.text: that he is mad and delusional
that he has murdered people before
that he is not mad, but dreadfully nervous
that he loves the old man
that he is planning to confess

starterQuiz.stem: Why does the narrator hate the old man in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
starterQuiz.hint: The narrator tells us: " I loved the old man. He had never wronged me. He had never given me insult. For his gold I had no desire."
starterQuiz.feedback: The narrator's motive for murdering the old man shows us his delusion.

options.text: because he is richer than him
because he disturbs him with loud music
because he is older and wiser than him
because he has a strange blue eye
because he was rude to him once

starterQuiz.stem: Hubristic means ...
starterQuiz.hint: Victor Frankenstein in 'Frankenstein' is a hubristic protagonist.
starterQuiz.feedback: The narrator in 'The Tell-Tale Heart' is extremely hubristic. This is a common trait of Gothic protagonists.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following words can be used as a synonym for 'suspense'?
starterQuiz.hint: Substitute each answer option into this sentence: The writer creates ...... by using repetition.
starterQuiz.feedback: Tension and suspense both mean 'the feelings of anxiety and excitement a reader may feel when they are unsure as to what might happen next'.

starterQuiz.stem: Complete the quotation from 'The Tell-Tale Heart': "He had the eye of a {{}}—a pale blue eye, with a film over it."
starterQuiz.hint: These creatures are repulsive scavengers who feed on the bodies of dead animals.
starterQuiz.feedback: Poe's use of this simile shows us the narrator's disgust with the old man's eye.

starterQuiz.stem: Starting with the first, put the quotations from 'The Tell-Tell Heart' in chronological order.
starterQuiz.hint: The first quotation is the narrator informing us that he will tell us a story. The last quotation will be his confession.
starterQuiz.feedback: Each of these quotations show us the narrator's escalating delusions.

order.text: "Hearken! and observe how healthily—how calmly I can tell you the whole story."
"I knew what the old man felt, and pitied him, although I chuckled at heart"
"There came to my ears a low, dull, quick sound, such as a watch makes"
"In an instant I dragged him to the floor, and pulled the heavy bed over him."
"I dismembered the corpse. I cut off the head and the arms and the legs.."
"The officers were satisfied. My manner had convinced them."
"Tear up the planks!—here, here!—It is the beating of his hideous heart!”"

exitQuiz.stem: What is meany by the term 'point of view'?
exitQuiz.hint: If someone asks you for your point of view, they are asking you for your.....?
exitQuiz.feedback: In 'The Tell-Tale Heart', the point of view the story is told from is that of the narrator's.

options.text: the perspective the text is told from
the tone of the narrative voice
the events that take place in the story

exitQuiz.stem: Which three words best describe the narrator in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
exitQuiz.hint: The narrator insists throughout the story that he is not 'mad'.
exitQuiz.feedback: The narrator's delusions make him unreliable and unpredictable.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following quotations from 'The Tell-Tale Heart' best shows us how dangerous the narrator is?
exitQuiz.hint: This quotation shows the narrator's cruelty and lack of remorse for the terror he is inflicting upon the old man.
exitQuiz.feedback: The joy that the narrator gets from tormenting the old man shows us how dangerous he is.

options.text: “But you should have seen me. You should have seen how wisely I proceeded”
“They heard!...they knew!—they were making a mockery of my horror!”
“Ha!—would a madman have been so wise as this?”
"I knew what the old man felt, and pitied him, although I chuckled at heart."

exitQuiz.stem: In 'The Tell-Tale Heart' Poe uses {{}} to create suspense. The narrator insists that he is not 'mad' but his heinous actions suggest otherwise.
exitQuiz.hint: The missing word means 'the expression of meaning by using language that suggests the opposite of the reality'.
exitQuiz.feedback: There is a dark comedy to this short story created through Poe's use of irony.

exitQuiz.stem: What is the effect of Poe's use of short sentences in this quotation from 'The Tell-Tale Heart': "“Almighty God!—no, no! They heard!—they suspected!—they knew!”?
exitQuiz.hint: This quotation is taken from the end of the story, before the narrator confesses to his heinous crime.
exitQuiz.feedback: Poe uses the short, exclamatory sentences to reflect the narrator's escalating delusions and loss of control.

options.text: The shorter sentences reflect the narrator's loss of control and hysteria.
The short sentences reflect the old man's time running out.
The short sentences reflect the narrator's lack of patience with the police.
The short sentences reflect the narrator's clarity and sanity in this moment.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following best explain why Poe used an unreliable narrator in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
exitQuiz.hint: Poe uses the unreliable narrator to create tension. How does this work?
exitQuiz.feedback: The narrator is also arguably a typical Gothic protagonist - seemingly isolated and egotistical.

options.text: Using an unreliable narrator makes us question whether the old man really died.
Using an unreliable narrator puts us in a state of discomfort and doubt.
The narrator's unreliability makes him a wicked, but likeable protagonist.
The narrator's unreliability makes him unpredictable, which creates suspense.
The narrator's unreliability makes him charismatic and endearing.

lessons.title: Symbolism in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'
lessons.outcome: I can identify and explain key symbols in ‘The Tell-Tale Heart’.
keyLearningPoints: Symbolism is where writers use objects, characters, or elements in their work, to represent deeper ideas and themes.
Poe uses the old man’s eye to symbolise intrusion, truth and moral or spiritual judgement in the story.
Poe uses the heart beat to symbolise the narrator’s guilt, paranoia and time running out.
Symbols allow the writer to communicate hidden or deeper meanings within the text.
When writing about a writer’s use of symbolism, it is always important to discuss why it has been used.

keywords.definition: where writers use objects, characters, or elements in their work, to represent deeper ideas and themes
the idea that people are morally-judged by a higher, spiritual being
if something recurs, it repeatedly occurs - it keeps happening
when someone wrongfully enters a space they shouldn’t be - this can be physical or metaphorical space

starterQuiz.stem: What is a symbol?
starterQuiz.hint: The love heart is symbolic of romantic relationships.
starterQuiz.feedback: A symbol is an object that represents an idea. For example, a dove is usually used as a symbol for peace.

options.text: a character who represents an approach
an object that represents an idea
an object that represents the characters

starterQuiz.stem: At which points in 'The Tell-Tale Heart' does the narrator hear the beating heart of the old man?
starterQuiz.hint: Read the answer options carefully. There are subtle differences between the times you have been given.
starterQuiz.feedback: The beating heart is a recurring symbol in the story.

options.text: in the beginning when he spies on the old man
when he sneaks into the old man's room and is hiding in wait to kill him
when the police first arrive at the house, just after he has killed the old man
when the police have sat down and are conversing with the narrator

starterQuiz.stem: Which words are used to describe the old man's eye in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
starterQuiz.hint: The animal that Poe compares to the old man's eye is a predatory animal that feeds on the carcasses of other dead animals.
starterQuiz.feedback: By describing the eye in this way, Poe creates a repulsive image of the old man's eye.

starterQuiz.stem: Robbers intrude on people's homes. What might 'to intrude' mean?
starterQuiz.hint: The narrator in the 'The Tell-Tale Heart' intrudes on the old man's privacy.
starterQuiz.feedback: You can intrude physically (by entering a space you are not supposed to be in) or metaphorically (you can intrude on someone's privacy by going through their phone).

options.text: to enter somewhere you are not supposed to be
to say something you are not supposed to say
to take something that is not yours
to move something away from its correct home

starterQuiz.stem: How does the narrator in 'The Tell-Tale Heart' murder the old man?
starterQuiz.hint: We are told: "In an instant I dragged him to the floor, and pulled the heavy ... over him."
starterQuiz.feedback: The narrator violates the old man with his own possessions, in a supposedly-safe and private space. This shows the brutal nature of his crime.

options.text: he stabs him and then lets him bleed out
he strangles him with his bare hands
he hits him over the head with a floor board
he smothers him with his own bed

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following quotations best shows the narrator's hysteria and loss of control in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
starterQuiz.hint: Remember, that Poe used shorter sentences and exclamation marks to reflect the narrator's escalating delusion.
starterQuiz.feedback: Poe uses the narrator's short, quick, exclamatory sentences to indicate his loss of control and descent into paranoid madness.

options.text: "But even yet I refrained and kept still. I scarcely breathed."
"Oh God! what could I do? I foamed—I raved—I swore!"
"Upon the eighth night I was more than usually cautious in opening the door. "

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following is not a theme in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
exitQuiz.hint: Work your way through each answer option and try to think of an example of it in the text. This will help you work out which theme does not feature.
exitQuiz.feedback: There are no clear familial connections in this text, so family is not a theme.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following are explanations of the symbolism of eyes in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider why the narrator fears the old man's eye so much.
exitQuiz.feedback: The narrator may be frightened of the old man's eye because it forces him to confront a truth about himself that he hates: that he is delusional.

options.text: eyes represent a lack of clarity - what the narrator cannot see
eyes represent hatred and fear because the narrator hates the old man
eyes represent moral or spiritual judgement and this frightens the narrator
eyes represent truth and the idea of seeing someone for who they truly are
eyes represent guidance and support, as the eye guides the narrator

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following quotations from 'The Tell-Tale Heart' best supports the idea that the old man's eye symbolises spiritual judgement?
exitQuiz.hint: Which quotation best shows the narrator's fear of the eye watching or judging him in some way?
exitQuiz.feedback: The fact that the eye "chilled the very marrow in [his] bones" could suggest that the watchful gaze of the eye penetrated the narrator to his core and therefore saw the narrator for who he truly was.

options.text: "I kept quite still and said nothing"
"here, here!—It is the beating of his hideous heart!”
"dull blue with a hideous veil over it that chilled the very marrow in my bones"
"it was not the old man who vexed me, but his Evil Eye"

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following does the sound of the beating heart in 'The Tell-Tale Heart' not symbolise?
exitQuiz.hint: Think about what heart beats sound like, and what they can represent.
exitQuiz.feedback: The persistent sound of the old man's heart beat drives the narrator to confession.

options.text: time running out for the old man
time running out for the narrator
the knock of the police on the door

exitQuiz.stem: If the beating heart in 'The Tell-Tale Heart' represents the narrator's guilt, then what point might Poe be trying to suggest about guilt?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider the effect that guilt has on the narrator - it forces him to confess his crimes.
exitQuiz.feedback: The narrator, despite speaking "in a high key and with violent gesticulations" cannot disguise the imagined sound of the beating heart. This shows that guilt is inescapable and cannot be hidden - it will always haunt a person.

options.text: that guilt is fleeting and passes with time
that guilt is an emotion that everybody has to experience in their life
that guilt is an emotion that can be ignored in the moment
that guilt is inescapable and will haunt a person
that guilt always drives a person to insanity

exitQuiz.stem: Why might a writer use symbolism?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider what the symbolism of the heart beat in 'The Tell-Tale Heart' conveys to the reader. What do we gain from it?
exitQuiz.feedback: In 'The Tell-Tale Heart', Poe uses the heart beat to symbolise an emotion the narrator has not fully realised yet.

options.text: to make their text more sophisticated and impressive
to make the reading experience more multi-sensory for the reader
to reveal hidden or deeper meanings to the reader
to reflect the various characters in the story
to move the plot along in the story

lessons.title: Planning a cohesive argument about 'The Tell-Tale Heart'

starterQuiz.stem: Complete the quotation from 'The Tell-Tale Heart': “Villains!” I shrieked, “dissemble no more! I admit the deed!—tear up the planks!—here, here!—It is the beating of his {{}} heart!”
starterQuiz.hint: The missing word can be a synonym for ugly.
starterQuiz.feedback: The quotation "hideous heart" shows us the narrator's delusion, as we see his fixation on the deceased old man's heart take over his sanity.

starterQuiz.stem: What is the effect of Poe using an unreliable narrator in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
starterQuiz.hint: What does the word 'unreliable' actually mean? If you had an unreliable friend, how might this affect you?
starterQuiz.feedback: Using an unreliable narrator puts the reader in a constant state of uncertainty and anxiety that is very typical of Gothic literature.

options.text: It creates a likeable and relatable protagonist for the reader to root for.
It adds an element of mystery because we cannot trust what he says to be true.
It creates tension because we never know what he might do next.
It creates a more Gothic text because Gothic protagonists are always unreliable.
It allows Poe to be more creative with the plot and make it more dynamic.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following words can be used as a synonym for 'insane'?
exitQuiz.hint: Try applying these words to the narator from 'The Tell-Tale Heart'.
exitQuiz.feedback: We should be careful how we use the words 'deranged' and 'deluded' as they can be condemning.

exitQuiz.stem: Which piece of vocabulary best describes the narrator's crimes in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
exitQuiz.hint: This word means appallingly-wicked and evil.
exitQuiz.feedback: We use the word 'heinous' in very extreme cases because it is a very strong word. It is a good word choice to describe the narrator's crimes because they are extremely violent.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following does not need to be included in the supporting detail in a paragraph outline?
exitQuiz.hint: One of the answer options does not need to be in an essay at all, as we can assume our reader is somewhat familiar with the text.
exitQuiz.feedback: Showing understanding of the plot is a more basic skill than being able to analyse the text - we need to focus our efforts on our analysis.

options.text: potential vocabulary you might want to use
the effects of the writer's use of methods

exitQuiz.stem: What is Poe's message about guilt in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
exitQuiz.hint: Consider what effect the narrator's own guilt has upon him in the text.
exitQuiz.feedback: Poe illustrates the destructive nature of guilt in the short story, by showing us how it drives the narrator to insanity.

options.text: that guilt is the product of insanity and needs to be processed healthily
that guilt is inescapable and can drive a person to insanity if unresolved
that guilt is a normal human emotion that we must learn to handle
that humans shouldn't have to feel guilt - it is an unnecessary emotion

exitQuiz.stem: What is the effect of this quotation from 'The Tell-Tale Heart': “It grew louder—louder—louder!”?
exitQuiz.hint: Read the quotation out loud and listen to how it sounds.
exitQuiz.feedback: Poe's use of dashes also helps to create the sound of a heartbeat. The dashes create the pause between the heart beats.

options.text: The dashes represent the narrator taking deep breaths between each noise.
The repetition shows the persistence of the narrator’s delusions.
“Louder” has two syllables, like a beating heart, so it's almost onomatopoeic.
The simile shows us how overwhelming the sound of the heart beating was.
The exclamation mark shows the narrator's enthusiasm for the noise.

exitQuiz.stem: What is the effect of this quotation from 'The Tell-Tale Heart': “I foamed—I raved—I swore!”?
exitQuiz.hint: Poe characterises the narrator as hysterical and out of control here. How?
exitQuiz.feedback: Poe uses verbs that are have been historically associated with madness to characterise the narrator as out of control and deranged.

options.text: "Swore" characterises the narrator as a rude and dislikeable person.
“Foamed” might remind us of a rabid dog - connotations of disease and madness
"Raved" shows how excited the narrator was - e.g "raving" about something
The triple shows the narrator’s escalating panic and stress
The pronoun "I" shows the narrator's selfishness, as he only thinks of himself

lessons.title: A written analysis of 'The Tell-Tale Heart'
lessons.outcome: I can confidently draft, and redraft a written analysis of a literary text.
keyLearningPoints: It is important to consider the first version of your work a first draft and not the finished essay.
Redrafting your critical writing is just as important as redrafting your creative writing.
A clear and concise essay focuses on the writer’s use of methods.
Successful essays offer a comprehensive explanation and exploration of the effects the writer’s methods.
Short, embedded quotations make your essay more concise and coherent.

keywords.definition: rewriting your work to improve it
any conscious choice the writer makes - this could be using a simile or choosing a specific word
using as few words as possible to express as much meaning as possible
not absolute, certain or agreed

equipment: You will need access to the short story 'The Tell-Tale Heart' by Edgar Allan Poe. You can find a copy of this in the additional materials.

starterQuiz.stem: What narrative perspective is 'The Tell-Tale Heart' written from?
starterQuiz.hint: Poe uses an unreliable narrator.
starterQuiz.feedback: The first person, unreliable narrator creates tension in the story.

starterQuiz.stem: What language method is used in the following quotation from 'The Tell-Tale Heart': "it is the beating of his hideous heart"?
starterQuiz.hint: Focus on the words 'hideous heart'. Both begin with a letter 'h'.
starterQuiz.feedback: Poe uses alliteration to highlight the narrator's disgust with the heart in this moment.

starterQuiz.stem: Complete the quotation from 'The Tell-Tale Heart': "True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am ...?"
starterQuiz.hint: The narrator denies being this throughout the story.
starterQuiz.feedback: The narrator persistently denies being 'mad', but his protestations and actions make us feel he may be lying.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is not an example of the writer's method?
starterQuiz.hint: The writer's method is any conscious choice the writer makes within the text.
starterQuiz.feedback: The publisher a writer chooses would not form part of their methods, as this doesn't affect the content of the text.

starterQuiz.stem: Complete the quotation from 'The Tell-Tale Heart': "To think that there I was, opening the door, little by little, and he not even to dream of my secret deeds or thoughts. I fairly {{ }} at the idea".
starterQuiz.hint: The narrator laughs in this moment. Can you think of any synonyms for 'laughed'?
starterQuiz.feedback: The moment where the narrator "chuckled" shows his insanity as he gets pleasure out of the old man's fear.

starterQuiz.stem: Match the key vocabulary up to its definition.
starterQuiz.hint: Start with irrational. If someone behaves irrationally, then their behaviour is....
starterQuiz.feedback: These are all words that you can use in your analysis of 'The Tell-Tale Heart'.

match.left: wicked and appaling
to be hidden
to not be of sound mind
horrified and shocked
not based upon logic or reason

exitQuiz.stem: Which question word forces you to think about the writer's use of methods?
exitQuiz.hint: The method to make biscuits is ..... you make them.
exitQuiz.feedback: If the question word is 'how', a strong focus on the writer's use of methods is required.

exitQuiz.stem: Which piece of punctuation does Poe use to show the narrator's escalating delusions in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
exitQuiz.hint: Poe uses these particularly at the end of the short story just before the narrator confesses to his hideous crimes.
exitQuiz.feedback: The use of exclamation marks reflects the narrator's loss of control at the end of the story.

exitQuiz.stem: If an essay is concise, what does this mean?
exitQuiz.hint: Essays are often written in timed conditions, which is why it is important to be concise.
exitQuiz.feedback: Being concise also makes your essay more clear and coherent, as you do not overcomplicate things by using too many words.

options.text: it uses as many words as possible to express as little meaning as possible
it uses as few words as possible to express as little meaning as possible
it uses as few words as possible to express as much meaning as possible
it uses as many words as possible to express as much meaning as possible

exitQuiz.stem: The writer's {{ }} is any decision that the writer makes consciously.
exitQuiz.hint: Examples of this might be using a simile, or choosing the word "gasped" instead of "inhaled".
exitQuiz.feedback: The writer's method can range from choosing a specific structure, to making a single word choice.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following are examples of embedded quotations?
exitQuiz.hint: An embedded quotation sits within the grammatical framework of the sentence.
exitQuiz.feedback: Using embedded quotations makes your essay more concise, as you only use the part of the quotation you want to analyse.

options.text: The narrator tells us: "I felt that I must scream"....
The narrator said he "felt" that "I must scream"...

exitQuiz.stem: What is the effect of this quotation from 'The Tell-Tale Heart': "I gasped for breath—and yet the officers heard it not"?
exitQuiz.hint: What emotions might lead a person to "gasp" for air?
exitQuiz.feedback: This quotation shows the narrator’s delusion as the imagined sound of the heartbeat causes him to lose all of his self-composure and hysterically confess to his crimes.

options.text: “Gasped” here shows the narrator’s sheer panic and loss of control.
"Gasped" shows that the feels suffocated by his delusions.
"Gasped" shows that the narrator is appalled by the police officers.
"Gasped" shows how excited the narrator is for his crimes to be discovered.

lessons.title: Analysing effective opinion articles
lessons.outcome: I can identify the features of effective opinion writing.
keyLearningPoints: The form of a piece is the kind of writing it is.
The form of a piece informs the tone you use.
Opinion writing requires a strong sense of voice and a persuasive tone.
Puns can be used in opinion writing to create wit.
Wit engages the reader, thereby making your piece more persuasive.

keywords.definition: the type of text you are writing
the identity of the writer that comes through the text
the attitude your words imply - the way in which you say something
a small joke (usually a play on words) made to create wit
using words in a quick and inventive way to create humour

equipment: You will need access to a copy of the model answer for this lesson, which is provided in the additional materials.

starterQuiz.stem: If you are expressing your opinion, you are expressing your....
starterQuiz.hint: Substitute each answer option into the above sentence and see which makes most sense.
starterQuiz.feedback: Your opinions are your ideas and beliefs.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is a kind of form of a text?
starterQuiz.hint: The form is what kind of text a piece of writing is.
starterQuiz.feedback: It is important to be aware of what form you are writing in, so that you can adhere to conventions of that form.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is not an example of a persuasive device?
starterQuiz.hint: These are all linguistic devices, but not all are persuasive linguistic devices.
starterQuiz.feedback: Onomatopoeia is not commonly used for being persuasive - it is used in persuasive writing, but it is not a persuasive method in itself.

starterQuiz.stem: Who is the audience for an opinion piece?
starterQuiz.hint: Before we start writing, we have to consider the form, audience and purpose of the task.
starterQuiz.feedback: The audience of a piece of writing are the intended readers of the piece of writing.

options.text: the person who is writing the piece of writing
the people reading the piece of writing
the people the writer may quote in their writing
the person the writing is about

starterQuiz.stem: What linguistic method has been used in the following quotation: "This is a problem that has crept up on us stealthily."?
starterQuiz.hint: Something that is not an animal, is being described in an animalistic way.
starterQuiz.feedback: Using zoomorphism to describe issues can make them seem more pressing and can make your reader want to take action against them.

starterQuiz.stem: What is the effect of the following quotation: "We must not rest, we must not become complacent; we must act...now."?
starterQuiz.hint: Read the sentence out loud and consider how it makes you feel.
starterQuiz.feedback: Using a triple, combined with the inclusive pronoun "we" can be a great way to persuade your reader.

options.text: It makes the reader feel part of something important.
It conveys a sense of urgency to the reader.
The repetition emphasises the importance of action.
It puts the responsibility for action on the writer.

exitQuiz.stem: {{ }} is the identity of the writer of a text and how this is conveyed.
exitQuiz.hint: This is how you express your opinions.
exitQuiz.feedback: Opinion writing requires a strong sense of voice.

exitQuiz.stem: {{ }} is the attitude you imply through your use of words.
exitQuiz.hint: When you are speaking, you change your ..... to reflect your feelings and mood.
exitQuiz.feedback: It is important to be able to craft different tones in your writing.

exitQuiz.stem: What is a pun?
exitQuiz.hint: Saying that something in English is 'lit' would be a pun.
exitQuiz.feedback: Puns can be used to create wit.

options.text: a kind of punctuation used to indicate humour
a comparison made between two things that are not the same

exitQuiz.stem: What kind of tone would you expect to find in an opinion article?
exitQuiz.hint: When writing an opinion article, you are trying to get your reader to agree with you.
exitQuiz.feedback: Establishing a persuasive tone is essential in opinion writing. This can be done through using humour to get your reader onside.

exitQuiz.stem: How does the writer create a sarcastic tone in this quotation: "I have no doubt that his efforts were more than appreciated..."?
exitQuiz.hint: Read the sentence out loud and consider which specific part of the sentence forces you to adopt a sarcastic tone.
exitQuiz.feedback: Using ellipses is a great way to create a sarcastic tone.

exitQuiz.stem: Match the linguistic method up to the example.
exitQuiz.hint: Opinion as fact is where you express an opinion, but you make it sound like a fact. Start with this one first.
exitQuiz.feedback: These are all useful methods to use in opinion articles.

match.left: Is seeing it really all that different from reading it?

we children are not angels; we are not delicate little flowers

lessons.title: Using description in functional writing
lessons.outcome: I can use a description to create interesting functional writing.
keyLearningPoints: Functional writing that makes use of description is often stronger.
Anecdotes are brilliant for connecting to the reader through creating a shared experience.
Before writing an anecdote, consider what you want your reader to feel - choose your language accordingly.
A successful anecdote makes use of language to create vivid imagery for the reader, so they can share the experience.
Figurative language can be very persuasive when used effectively.

keywords.definition: a short, personal story told to illustrate a point
a group of words with shared meaning
language that is meaningful, but not literally true
easily-spread or transferred - usually used to describe illnesses or emotions

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the correct definition for 'figurative language'?
starterQuiz.hint: Similes and metaphors are examples of kinds of figurative language.
starterQuiz.feedback: Figurative language can be extremely useful in functional writing to express urgency or spur the reader to action.

options.text: language that uses two or more similar sounds
language that indicates time or place
language that is meaningful but not literally true
language that sounds the noise it represents
language that requires prior knowledge to understand

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following methods are figurative language methods?
starterQuiz.hint: Which of these involve a comparison of two things that are not the same, but share similar qualities?
starterQuiz.feedback: Figurative language often compares two things that are not the same, but share similar qualities to create meaning.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the the following are examples of figurative language?
starterQuiz.hint: Figurative language is language that is meaningful but not literally true.
starterQuiz.feedback: Figurative language is a great way to create vivid imagery for your reader.

options.text: My name is Eleanor - Eleanor Snow.

The house was enormous - too big if I was honest.

starterQuiz.stem: If a writer uses an anecdote, what are they using?
starterQuiz.hint: You might use an anecdote to form a person connection to your reader.
starterQuiz.feedback: Anecdotes are short, personal stories told about a person's experiences with the topic. They help the writer to form a connection to the reader.

options.text: two or more words that begin with the same letter
a question that doesn't require an answer
words that sound like the noise they represent

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following openings is anecdotal?
starterQuiz.hint: An anecdote is a short personal story told in relation to the topic.
starterQuiz.feedback: Anecdotes can be a great way to start a piece of functional writing. They engage the reader instantly when done well.

options.text: My name is Ella. I'm 25 years old.
I've been a doctor all my life.

We've all watched the news, haven't we?

starterQuiz.stem: Match the rhetorical device to its definition.
starterQuiz.hint: Begin with anecdote. Here is an example of an anecdote: Last year, on my way to work....
starterQuiz.feedback: These are all useful devices in functional writing that can be used persuasively.

match.left: short personal story
a question that doesn't need an answer
a type of repetition at the start of successive clauses
using words like 'we' to create a community
repeating a word

exitQuiz.feedback: Anecdotes are brilliant for capturing the reader's attention at the beginning of a piece of functional writing.

exitQuiz.stem: What is the effect of using an anecdote in functional writing?
exitQuiz.hint: Telling a personal story creates a shared experience between you and your reader/audience.
exitQuiz.feedback: Anecdotes also show your reader where your passion for your topic comes from, which can be very persuasive.

options.text: they can illustrate your point in a different way
they can show your reader that you are a nice person
they can help you establish a connection to your reader
the can stop your audience from heckling you during a speech

exitQuiz.hint: This is language that is meaningful, but not literally true.
exitQuiz.feedback: Descriptive writing using figurative language can really enhance your functional writing.

exitQuiz.stem: A strong anecdote should....
exitQuiz.hint: Creating a shared experience with your reader requires them to feel what you feel.

options.text: only be told at the beginning of a piece of writing
only be told once in a piece of writing - it cannot be referred to again
use language methods to create vivid imagery for the reader
lead with emotions so that the reader/audience knows how to feel

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following is an example of a semantic field of restriction?
exitQuiz.hint: A semantic field is a group of words that all share a similar meaning.
exitQuiz.feedback: Each of these words shares a similar meaning - that of control and restriction.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of the following use figurative language to persuade?
exitQuiz.hint: Figurative language is language that is meaningful, but not literally true.
exitQuiz.feedback: The words 'imprisoned' and the phrase 'in tatters' are examples of figurative language because they are not literally true, but they used to illustrate the writer's point.

lessons.title: The structure of an opinion article
lessons.outcome: I can explain how to create engaging openings and impactful endings in an opinion piece.
keyLearningPoints: You can create an engaging opening by using humour, or creating a shared experience with your reader.
In an opinion piece, your message is your opinion.
In an opinion piece, it is important to get the reader onside, so that they are more likely to internalise your message.
The ending of your opinion piece should bring together the threads of your argument and reinforce your viewpoint.
You can create an impactful ending by using mirroring and/or leaving your reader with a moral conundrum to consider.

keywords.definition: memorable and significant.
to indicate the truth about something without explicitly saying it.
a person’s opinion or perspective on something.
to strengthen or further support something - in this context -  an idea.
a confusing and difficult-to-answer problem or question.

starterQuiz.stem: What is the 'form' of a piece of writing?

starterQuiz.feedback: Different forms of writing each follow their own set of rules.

options.text: using words in a quick and inventive way
the type of text being written
the tone of a piece of writing

starterQuiz.stem: In an opinion article, what kind of tone would you expect to find?
starterQuiz.hint: Think about the purpose of an opinion piece - you want your readers to agree with you.
starterQuiz.feedback: Creating a persuasive tone is crucial in opinion writing if you want your readers to agree with you.

starterQuiz.stem: What do we mean by the word 'structure' when we talk about the structure of a text?
starterQuiz.hint: When discussing structure we often look at openings and endings.
starterQuiz.feedback: Structuring an opinion article effectively can make it really engaging for your reader.

options.text: the tone of voice that is used in the text
the way the text is organised
the language devices the writer uses

starterQuiz.stem: What is being described here: 'The attitude your words imply - the way in which you say something.'?

starterQuiz.feedback: Learning how to craft different tones in your writing can help make your writing more engaging.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is not an example of a persuasive device?
starterQuiz.hint: These are all linguistic devices, but not all are used as persuasive devices.
starterQuiz.feedback: Personification is not known for being persuasive. It can be used in persuasive writing but it's not a persuasive device in itself.

starterQuiz.stem: What method is being used in the following sentence: “You never forget your first horror film.”?

starterQuiz.feedback: Anecdotes are a great way to build a connection with your reader.

exitQuiz.stem: What is the purpose of an opinion piece?
exitQuiz.hint: When giving your opinion you often want people to agree with you.

exitQuiz.stem: Why are engaging openings so important when writing an opinion article?

options.text: it shows your opinion is correct
it begins to get your reader onside
it allows you to show off your writing skills

exitQuiz.stem: Match the key terms to their definitions.

match.left: memorable and significant
to indicate the truth about something

a confusing and difficult-to-answer problem

lessons.title: Planning an opinion article about Gothic literature

starterQuiz.stem: What is a topic sentence?

starterQuiz.stem: Why were Victorian audiences so interested in Gothic literature?

units.title: Gothic poetry
units.description: In this unit, pupils read and explore two nineteenth-century gothic poems by Edgar Allen Poe. They first read and analyse 'The Raven' and 'The Haunted Palace' in isolation, before comparing them to each other and developing a personal response. Finally, they practise performing one of the poems.

keyLearningPoints: Edgar Allan Poe wrote brilliant ghost stories and detective fiction.

exitQuiz.stem: What is the best definition of nostalgic?

lessons.title: Performing your chosen Gothic poem
lessons.outcome: I can effectively deliver a Gothic poem using a range of performance techniques.
keyLearningPoints: Performing a poem means bringing out the drama of the poem.
It is important to vary the pace and tone in your performance.
It's best to learn the poem so you can perform the poem and not just say it.
You should make eye contact with the audience when performing a poem.
Peer-assessment is a useful tool to help each other make a range of improvements.

keywords.definition: a performance is a way of entertaining an audience with speech, acting or music
how speakers use their voice to convey their feelings is known as tone
to change your speaking pace is to change how quickly or slowly you speak
we call performers fluent if they speak without hesitation or mistakes

starterQuiz.feedback: To assail means to attack.

starterQuiz.stem: Match the imagery in 'The Haunted Palace' with their mostly likely meanings.

triumph
the self
destruction

the speed at which something happens

Use a bigger piece of paper so it is easier to read from.

Have someone hold up the paper so you can look up as you read.

treat it as a pause to draw attention to key words
treat it as a sign to speed up and speak faster

exitQuiz.stem: Why is peer assessment useful?

units.title: A history of language
units.description: In this unit, pupils explore the history of the English Language. They first learn about the development of the English Language, before using a single word and the Lord's Prayer to explore how language changes. They then plan, write and deliver a persuasive speech about a new word.

lessons.title: A history of the English language
lessons.outcome: I can explain how the English language has been influenced by different historical events over time.
keyLearningPoints: The invading Angles, Saxons and Jutes brought useful language, for describing everyday things.
The English population adopted Latin words through the Church and French words through the Norman invasion.
Both Shakespeare and the King James Bible gave the English language many of the phrases that we use today.
Scientific developments led to the creation of many new words.
The expansion of the British Empire led to new words being adopted and the English language travelling globally.

keywords.definition: To conquer means to take control of a particular place and its people by force.
To invade a country means to enter it by force with an army.
Colonisation occurs when a country takes control of other lands and its people and creates settlements there.
If a group adopt a new word, they start using it.

starterQuiz.stem: Who invaded England first?
starterQuiz.hint: The Normans invaded England as part of the battle of 1066.
starterQuiz.feedback: The Anglo-Saxons invaded England in the 5th century and the Normans invaded England in the 11th century.

starterQuiz.stem: When the Bible first arrived in England, what language was it written in?
starterQuiz.hint: This was the same language spoken in Ancient Rome.
starterQuiz.feedback: The first Christian missionaries arrived in the 2nd century with the Bible written in Latin.

starterQuiz.stem: In what century was William Shakespeare born?
starterQuiz.hint: William Shakespeare was born during the reign of Queen Elizabeth I.
starterQuiz.feedback: William Shakespeare was born in 1564.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the definition of conquer? Here it is used in a sentence: The army was able to conquer their enemies.
starterQuiz.hint: Use this extra sentence to help you define it: I was able to conquer my stage fright and give the presentation sucessfully.
starterQuiz.feedback: To conquer means to take control of a particular place and its people by defeating them.

starterQuiz.stem: Select the plays that were written by William Shakespeare.
starterQuiz.hint: Shakespeare usually named his plays after the main character.
starterQuiz.feedback: Both Hamlet and Romeo and Juliet were written by William Shakespeare.

starterQuiz.stem: Which of the following is the definition of adopt? Here it is used in a sentence: Over time, languages adopt new words.
starterQuiz.hint: Use this extra sentence to help you define it: As we invent new things, society adopts new words to describe them.
starterQuiz.feedback: If a language adopts a new word it means they acquire it.

exitQuiz.stem: Many words associated with law and government were introduced by the Normans.
exitQuiz.hint: The Normans retained 'Norman French' for important things like law and government.
exitQuiz.feedback: Words like 'judge', 'jury' and 'government' are all influenced by 'Norman French'.

options.text: True - they added 5000 words to the English language
True - they added 10000 words to the English language
False - the Anglo-Saxons added words associated with law to the English language
False - they only added words linked with food to the English language

exitQuiz.stem: The Anglo-Saxons mainly introduced words to describe ...
exitQuiz.hint: The Normans used 'Norman French' for political and legal systems which is why many legal words are influenced by 'Norman French'.
exitQuiz.feedback: The Anglo-Saxons introduced many common words for things like 'work', 'sleep' and 'house'.

exitQuiz.stem: The Bible was very influential in the development of the English language. Which reasons below explain why?
exitQuiz.hint: The invention of the printing press meant many more people could read the Bible. The Bible's stories were well-known and references to them were common. The Bible was read by people across all walks of life.
exitQuiz.feedback: The Bible was culturally significant. It had a widespread influence and it was very accessible.

exitQuiz.stem: Which of these did Shakespeare **not** do?
exitQuiz.hint: 'Break the ice' is an expression that Shakespeare created. He also introduced words like 'dwindle'.
exitQuiz.feedback: Shakespeare introduced new words and phrases; standardised spelling and grammar; and introduced many new phrases.

exitQuiz.stem: Which words below were added to the English language as a result of the British Empire?
exitQuiz.hint: One of the words is based on the Hindi word 'jangala'.
exitQuiz.feedback: The British Empire’s scale meant that many new things were encountered from other cultures and their words in English were heavily influenced by other languages (e.g. - kangaroo).

exitQuiz.stem: Which examples below are words added to the English language as a result of the Scientific Revolution of the 17th century?
exitQuiz.hint: The ‘Scientific Revolution’ was a time when scientists made big discoveries in science and started using a new way of thinking called the scientific method.
exitQuiz.feedback: Scientists discovered lots of new things that needed naming (like 'electricity') and also needed precision in their experiments, leading to the creation of words like 'hypothesis'.

lessons.title: Reading an Anglo-Saxon Bible extract
lessons.outcome: I can use reading skills to comprehend an extract from the Bible written in Old English.
keyLearningPoints: The Anglo-Saxons inhabited Great Britain from the 5th Century.
The Anglo-Saxons included people from Germanic tribes, who migrated from mainland Europe.
The Anglo-Saxons were very important in the development of Old English.
Whilst a lot of words have changed over the years, modern words linked to the church are similar to Old English.
A noun appositive is a phrase that gives a piece of extra information about a noun.

keywords.definition: The Anglo-Saxons were Germanic tribes that conquered England in the 5th century.
Old English was an early version of English spoken in the Middle Ages.
To translate something means to change it from one language to another.
If something is forbidden it is not allowed.
A paradise is a place of great happiness. It can also refer to heaven.

starterQuiz.stem: 'Old {{}}' was the language spoken in Britain between the 5th and 12th centuries.

starterQuiz.feedback: Old English was spoken in England between the 5th and 12th centuries.

options.text: A noun is a word used to describe an action, state or occurence.

options.text: To improve the language in a piece of writing.

Moon
Book

lessons.title: Comparing the Lord's Prayer over time
lessons.outcome: I can compare different versions of the Lord’s Prayer and explain how language has changed over time.
keyLearningPoints: The Lord's Prayer, from the King James Bible 1611, contains many words that we still use today.
Modern technologies have caused us to use abbreviations as part of spoken language.
New words are created all the time, with generational divides between word usage.

keywords.definition: If something is hallowed then it is very respected because of its importance.
If something is outdated then it is old-fashioned and no longer considered current.
A generation refers to all of the people born and living at about the same time.
If something occurs across generations it can be described as intergenerational.
An abbreviation is a shortened form of a word or phrase.

starterQuiz.feedback: The Anglo-Saxons are more responsible for the creation of Old English.

starterQuiz.hint: Many monks continued to speak and teach in Latin after the Norman conquest.
starterQuiz.feedback: Words associated with religion are very similar in modern English, old English and Latin.

starterQuiz.stem: What was the name of the language spoken in England between the 5th and 12th centuries?

starterQuiz.stem: Match the below keywords with their definitions.

lessons.title: Exploring how a word's meaning can change over time
lessons.outcome: I can explain how the meanings of words can change over time.
keyLearningPoints: Weakening is when a word is overused and loses the strength of its meaning
Intensification is when a word acquires a stronger meaning over time
Amelioration is when a word acquires a certain, more pleasurable meaning than it once had
Pejoration is when a word acquires negative connotations that it did not have before

keywords.definition: When a word is overused and its meaning is altered this is called weakening.
When a word acquires a stronger meaning than it had before this is called intensification.
Amelioration is when a word acquires pleasant connotations that it didn’t have before.
Pejoration is when a word acquires negative connotations that it didn’t have before.
A superlative shows the highest or lowest quality of something. e.g 'best' or 'greatest'.

starterQuiz.stem: In which language was the Lord's Prayer first said?

Tyndale Bible
King James Bible

options.text: A word that shows the highest or lowest quality of something

starterQuiz.feedback: An abbreviation is a shortened form of words and phrases that convey the same meaning in fewer words (e.g. ‘Tbc’ instead of ‘To be continued’)

starterQuiz.stem: If something occurs across generations then it can be described as ....

match.left: when a word acquires a more negative meaning
a process when a word acquires a more pleasant meaning

options.text: Its meaning has changed from well-known to well-known but for negative reasons

lessons.title: Creating a new word
lessons.outcome: I can create a new word using specific language change techniques.
keyLearningPoints: Blending is when words are 'chopped up' and put together.
Compounds are when two words are merged (sometimes using a hyphen).
Initialism is like an acronym, except all the letters are pronounced.
Affixation means fastening parts of words to other words.

keywords.definition: In language, blending means to join the beginning of one word with the end of another to create a new word.
Compounds are words that are formed by combining two existing words together.
An acronym is a word formed by combining the first letter of each word in a name or phrase (e.g. ASAP).
Initialism is an abbreviation where the first letters of each word are pronounced as separate letters (e.g. CCTV).
Affixation is the process of adding groups of letters to the beginning or ends of words to change their meanings.

starterQuiz.stem: Where does a prefix come in a word?

starterQuiz.feedback: A prefix comes at the start of a word.

starterQuiz.feedback: The definition of the word initial is existing or occurring at the beginning.

options.text: Existing or occurring at the beginning.

lessons.title: Planning a persuasive speech about a new word

keyLearningPoints: A successful speech will maintain a clear, single viewpoint throughout.
Ideas must be logically sequenced and linked, so that the audience can follow the argument.
Vocabulary and language devices must be chosen for effect.
Use structural features at paragraph and sentence level, to manage pace and emphasis.

keywords.definition: A viewpoint refers to a person’s point of view on a particular issue.

lessons.title: Writing a persuasive speech about a new word

keyLearningPoints: Rhetorical questions, anecdotes and direct address are a great way to ‘hook’ your audience at the start of a speech.
The content of a speech needs to be sufficiently developed for the argument to be convincing.
Language devices should be creative, original and matched to the purpose and audience of a speech.

keywords.definition: If a speech is convincing then it is able to persuade someone of the merits of something.
